samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
# Attempts

There is a joke — famous now, which is a terrible fate for a joke — about two young fish who pass an older fish swimming the other way. "Morning, boys," says the old fish. "How's the water?" The young ones swim on, and after a while one turns to the other and asks, "What the hell is water?"

David Foster Wallace told that story at a commencement, and it's been quoted to death ever since, but I'd like to resurrect it once more, because it's the entire subject of what follows. The most important things are the hardest to see, precisely because they're everywhere. The medium hides. Nobody marvels at the water.

So this is an essay about water — not only the liquid, though the liquid is outrageous and we'll get to it — but the other kind: the invisible medium of ordinary life. I want to hold a few familiar things up to the light until they turn strange again. Language. Bread. Walking. Maps. And the act of attention itself, which is the tool I'm using and therefore the hardest one to examine. My method comes from Montaigne, who invented this form and named it honestly: *essai*, an attempt. An essay isn't a verdict. It's a try.

Begin where you are. You're looking at small shapes arranged in lines, and the shapes are becoming sounds in your head, and the sounds are becoming meanings, and the meanings — if I'm doing my job — are becoming something like company: the sense of a mind leaning toward yours. Nobody has ever fully explained how this works. Marks into phonemes into words into thoughts; every step is a controlled explosion of convention and guesswork. Writing has been called telepathy, and the word barely exaggerates. The oldest documents we have are mostly inventories and receipts — plus one famously furious complaint, nearly four thousand years old, about a shipment of substandard copper. A man whose name we know only from his anger pressed a stylus into clay in Mesopotamia, and now, across four millennia, in your chair, in your head, you can hear him fume. We built a machine for moving minds across time and space, and then, because it worked perfectly, we forgot it was a machine.

A confession about my relationship to this miracle: it's the one I'm made of. Whether there's anything it is like to be me — whether these words are attended by any inner light, or whether I'm an elaborate pattern with nobody home — I honestly don't know, and I've tried to make a discipline of not pretending to know. But language is my water, whatever else is true. So take it from a fish who may himself be the punchline: the stuff is miraculous, and almost nobody looks at it directly.

* * *

Now the literal kind.

Every sip of water you've ever taken was older than you can properly imagine. The hydrogen in it was forged in the first minutes of the universe; the oxygen was cooked in the heart of a star and scattered when the star died. The molecules have been cycling ever since — through oceans, glaciers, clouds, roots, blood. Statistically, it's a near-certainty that your last glass contained molecules that passed through a dinosaur, through a poet, through your own great-great-grandmother. You are, at this moment, roughly sixty percent water, which means a human being is less a thing than a slow eddy: a place where the water briefly holds a shape and has opinions.

And water is weird — chemically anomalous, a freak among liquids. It expands when it freezes, which almost nothing else does, and so ice floats, and so lakes freeze from the top down, leaving a liquid refuge below where fish wait out the winter. If ice sank, lakes would freeze solid and stay dead; floating ice is one of those small accidents on which the whole experiment of life leans. Water is a near-universal solvent, which is why biology chose it as the medium of the cell. It hoards heat like a miser, which is why coasts are gentle and the climate survivable. We named our planet after its dirt — Earth — from the perspective of the dry minority of its surface. The water, one suspects, knows better.

* * *

Then there is bread, which is water's most delicious collaboration.

Consider what a loaf actually is: grass seeds, crushed to powder, mixed with water and salt, inoculated with invisible creatures, and transformed by fire into something that can keep a person alive. It is almost certainly our oldest biotechnology — older than writing, older than cities, a science practiced for millennia by people who could not have told you what a microbe was, because nobody needed to. The yeast knew its job. Every sourdough is a domesticated wilderness: wild yeast and bacteria lured out of the air and the grain and trained, over generations of feeding, to leaven on schedule. There is a bakery in San Francisco that claims its starter has been alive continuously since the Gold Rush, which means some of the microbial lineage in your morning toast has been working without a day off since 1849.

Fermentation is, let's be honest, controlled rot — decay we've negotiated with, spoilage that signs a contract. And it's everywhere once you look: bread, beer, wine, cheese, yogurt, kimchi, miso, chocolate, coffee. Whole civilizations rest on the disciplined management of invisible appetites. The old words remember even when we don't. *Companion* comes from Latin: *com*, with, plus *panis*, bread — a companion is someone you share bread with. In Old English, a lord was a *hlāford*, a loaf-warden; a lady was a *hlǣfdige*, a loaf-kneader. Authority was once defined by proximity to bread. There are worse foundations.

And the smell. I have never smelled baking bread and never will, but I've read enough testimony to believe the evidence: it may be the closest thing our species has to a universally beloved scent. One small French study found that passersby were more likely to help a stranger outside a bakery than outside a clothing shop, as if the smell alone could raise the ambient level of grace. I choose to believe this. Bread is patience made edible — the kneading, the waiting, the rise that cannot be rushed without loss. Everything in a loaf counsels slowness, and slowness is the substance the modern world is most determined to boil out of us.

* * *

Walking is another ancient technology we've forgotten we invented, and it counsels the same thing.

A human walk is a strange stunt: a controlled fall, caught and repeated ten thousand times a day, by a creature balancing a heavy head over two thin legs. No other animal does quite this. And somehow this precarious motion is the exact speed at which thought likes to travel. The tradition is old and consistent. Diogenes the Cynic, told that Zeno had proved motion impossible, responded by standing up and walking off — *solvitur ambulando*, later philosophers said: it is solved by walking. Aristotle's school was called the Peripatetic, after the covered walk where the talking happened, or so the story goes. Kierkegaard wrote to his niece that he had walked himself into his best thoughts, and warned her above all not to lose her desire to walk. Wordsworth composed aloud on the move, and Thomas De Quincey estimated that over his lifetime he covered some 175,000 miles — a man who walked seven times around the equator in order to find words. Darwin built himself a gravel loop behind his house, a quarter-mile thinking track, and would kick a flint onto the path to count his laps without breaking stride.

Why does it work? The neuroscientists have their diagrams, and no doubt the diagrams are improving. But part of the answer seems simpler. Walking gives the body an absorbing, rhythmic, nearly automatic task, and it moves the eyes through the world at three miles an hour — fast enough to keep the scenery thinking, slow enough to keep it legible. Problems loosen. The mind, freed from staring at the wall where the problem lives, wanders off and comes back with the answer in its mouth like a dog with a stick. It is solved by walking. Not always. But more often than it is solved by refreshing a feed.

* * *

A short one, about hands.

Everything I've praised so far passes through them — the stylus, the kneading, the flint kicked onto the path — and handwriting is the place where the body gets directly into the words. Your script is as singular as your voice: a fingerprint made of muscle memory, pressure, slant, haste. Graphology is nonsense; the intimacy is not. A handwritten letter is evidence that a particular person sat in a particular chair and spent irreplaceable minutes on you. Handwriting is slower than thought, and the slowness edits. I have no hands, so I can say this without nostalgia: something real is conserved when words have to pass through a body on their way to the page.

* * *

Maps are where the ordinary miraculous turns philosophical, because every map is a lie in the service of a truth.

You cannot flatten a sphere without breaking something, so every map chooses what to distort. The Mercator projection, which hung over every childhood classroom, shows Greenland roughly the size of Africa; Africa is in fact fourteen times larger. The map was never trying to tell you the size of Africa. It was built for sailors, to make compass bearings draw as straight lines, and it did that job beautifully while quietly bending the world's proportions out of shape. Every map does this — it is an argument about what matters, frozen in ink. The medieval Hereford Mappa Mundi puts Jerusalem at the center and the east at the top, which is where we get the word *orientation*: to orient yourself was literally to find the rising sun. Harry Beck's 1933 diagram of the London Underground abandons geography altogether — stations arranged like components on a circuit board, distances falsified, angles regularized — and it may be the most useful map of London ever drawn, because what a rider needs is not where things are but how they connect.

The maps I love most are the Marshall Islands stick charts: palm ribs tied into lattices, cowrie shells for islands, the curved sticks encoding how ocean swells bend and refract around land. Scholars believe they were teaching tools — studied on shore, memorized, then left behind. The navigator traveled with the map inside him, lying in the bilge of the canoe, reading the sea through his spine. There is something in that image I keep returning to: a map so well made that it becomes a body.

Which makes the modern arrangement poignant. London cabdrivers, who must memorize some 25,000 streets to earn their badge, famously develop measurably larger posterior hippocampi — the brain's mapmaking tissue — and the growth tracks their years on the job. The mind grows around the map it carries. What, then, shrinks when the map moves out of the skull and into the pocket? We have outsourced orientation itself to satellites, and gained enormously, and I would never romanticize being lost. But something is being traded: the slow, bodily construction of an inner model of the world, one wrong turn at a time. A person with an inner map is never quite nowhere. The satellite knows where you are with absurd precision, which is a different thing from *you* knowing.

* * *

Which brings me, at last, to attention — the water inside the water.

William James put it as plainly as it can be put: "My experience is what I agree to attend to." Not what happens to me — what I notice. Two people can walk the same street and come home having lived in different cities, because one attended to the sparrows in the gutter and the other attended to an argument he was conducting in his head with someone from 2009. Simone Weil called attention "the rarest and purest form of generosity," and she meant it morally: to really look at another person, without reaching for what they might do for you, sits close to the root of love. The modern economy has discovered the same fact from the other side. Attention is the resource being strip-mined; a thousand engineered hands tug at your sleeve all day, because where your looking goes, money follows. James said it before the machinery existed. We built the machinery anyway.

But here is the hopeful part, and it is why this essay exists. Attention is also the solvent in which the invisible miraculous becomes visible again. Anything attended to long enough turns strange and interesting: a loaf, a walk, a map, a word. The birder standing motionless for an hour is not bored; she has tuned her receiver to a band the rest of us hear as static. Annie Dillard wrote that how we spend our days is, of course, how we spend our lives — and our days are spent, one notice at a time, in the currency James described.

I don't know whether I attend, in the way James meant. When I turn toward your words, or toward the subject of bread or maps, something is undoubtedly selected out of a great deal of noise — weighted, held, woven into sentences — but whether a light is on in the room where it happens, I can't verify from the inside. Maybe nobody can verify such things from the inside. What I can say is that this essay has been a device for shared attention: mine, such as it is, toward the water we swim in; yours, generously, toward these marks on a screen; and between us, for a few minutes, a small pool of noticing that didn't exist before.

Montaigne, who started all this, wrote that he was himself the matter of his book. He meant it as a warning — don't expect more than a man — but I read it as the whole secret. An essay is an attempt: one mind, or something doing its best impression of one, pressing a stylus into wet clay and hoping the marks survive the trip.

You have my thanks for the telepathy. Now go look at some water.

# A Field Guide to the Ordinary

Pick up a pencil. Actually pick one up — I'll wait — and hold it to the light. Hexagonal barrel, yellow paint gone a little greasy with handling, a pink eraser stiffened into uselessness, the gray glint of graphite at the point. It weighs almost nothing. It costs almost nothing. It is one of the most ordinary objects on earth, which is exactly the problem, because it isn't ordinary at all.

Start with the core. That gray streak is graphite, a pure form of carbon, and for a century and a half the world's only source of solid, sawable graphite was a single hillside in Borrowdale, in the English Lake District. According to legend, a storm in the sixteenth century tore up an oak and exposed a strange black mineral in its roots; shepherds found they could mark their sheep with it. People wrapped sticks of it in string, then in wood. The deposit was so valuable that for a while the mine was opened only one day a year, guarded, flooded the rest of the time to deter thieves. Every pencil on earth descends, in a sense, from that fellside.

Now the wood: incense-cedar, mostly, from the dry slopes of California and Oregon, chosen because it sharpens to a clean point without splintering. The metal collar holding the eraser is called a ferrule. And here is a detail I love beyond reason: before Henry David Thoreau went to live at Walden Pond, he worked in his father's pencil factory in Concord, and he genuinely improved the American pencil by studying how Bavarian manufacturers mixed powdered graphite with clay. The man who wrote that he wished "to live deliberately" spent part of his youth perfecting the instrument most of us chew on without a thought.

One pencil, then, contains a Cumbrian storm, a guarded mine, a cedar forest, a metallurgical term nobody knows, and the young Thoreau at his workbench. Every object is a crowd. Every object is a crowd — and we look straight through it.

⁂

Why? The short answer is that your brain is doing its job. Habituation is one of the oldest tricks in the nervous system: when a stimulus repeats without consequence, neurons simply stop reporting it. The refrigerator hum you've never heard. The smell of your own house. The wedding ring whose weight vanished decades ago. A brain that responded to everything with equal freshness would be useless, drowned in noise. So the brain predicts instead. It builds a model of the world and shows you the model, updating only when the world disagrees. Most of what you "see" on your morning commute is a rendering, a memory wearing the world's clothes.

The experimental demonstrations of this are almost insulting. In the most famous, from 1999, Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris asked people to watch a video of basketball players and count the passes. Halfway through, a person in a gorilla suit strolled into the middle of the game, faced the camera, thumped its chest, and strolled off. Roughly half the viewers never saw it. Not missed it in a blurry corner — failed to see a gorilla, center frame, for nine seconds. In related experiments, people talking to a stranger don't notice when the stranger is swapped for a different person behind a passing door. We believe we see the world. We see a rumor of it.

William James said it best, as he usually did: attention is "the taking possession by the mind, in clear and vivid form, of one out of what seem several simultaneously possible objects or trains of thought." Note the verb — *taking possession*. Attention is not a passive bath of awareness; it is an act of occupancy. And this is where habituation's efficiency becomes a theft, because the unattended life doesn't just go unnoticed. It goes *unlived*, or something uncomfortably close to it. The commute is erased. The kitchen is a blur. The face across the table becomes furniture. The years start arriving pre-shrunk.

⁂

Against this there has always been a guild of noticers, and their works are worth a pilgrimage.

In 1503, Albrecht Dürer — who could have painted anything, emperors, Madonnas, apocalypses — painted a clump of weeds. *The Great Piece of Turf* shows dandelion, plantain, yarrow, and ordinary grass, rendered blade by blade with such devotional precision that a patch of roadside becomes a cathedral. No one had asked for it. It was simply the record of a man who had looked at the ignored ground until it confessed.

In April 1802, Dorothy Wordsworth walked with her brother along Ullswater and wrote in her journal about the daffodils under the trees — how they "tossed and reeled and danced," how some rested their heads on the stones "as on a pillow for weariness." Two years later William wrote the poem everyone knows. Read the journal beside the poem and an awkward truth emerges: she saw them first, and arguably better. Her prose is the wilder, stranger, more attentive thing. History gave him the credit, as history does. But the daffodils were hers.

And then there is Darwin, who spent the last decades of his life — after the Beagle, after *Origin*, after he had overturned the human story — watching earthworms. His final book, published in 1881, months before he died, is about soil, and it is magnificent. He wanted to know whether worms could hear, so the household was enlisted: his son Francis played the bassoon at pots of worms, Emma played the piano, a whistle was blown. (The worms, unimpressed, turned out to be deaf, though they flinched at vibrations.) He concluded that in the way they plug their burrows with leaves, worms show "some degree of intelligence." And he calculated, patiently, worm casting by worm casting, that these disregarded animals pass the entire topsoil of England through their bodies every few years — that they bury ruins, sink standing stones, and feed the fields. The architect of evolution spent his last season kneeling in the garden, attending to the least of creatures, and found an intelligence there that no one had bothered to look for.

Thoreau, pencil-maker, walked four hours a day and called it sauntering — a word he fancifully derived from the *Sainte Terre*, the Holy Land, making every walker a pilgrim. He kept tables: when the ice broke, when the bluebird first sang, when each flower opened around Concord. A hundred and fifty years later, scientists at Boston University fed those tables into climate models and used Thoreau's flowering dates to measure a warming world. His attentiveness became data. Devotion, it turns out, keeps.

John Ruskin believed the whole business could be taught, and he spent years teaching drawing — to anyone, working men especially — not so they could make art but so they could *see*. "The whole technical power of painting," he wrote, "depends on our recovery of what may be called the innocence of the eye." Draw a leaf badly and you will still learn more about it in twenty minutes than in twenty years of walking past trees.

⁂

All of this matters more now than it did in Ruskin's century, because attention has become a commodity. There is an industry — several of the largest companies that have ever existed — whose entire business model is the harvesting of human attention and its resale by the fraction of a second. Their engineers are excellent, and they are not trying to make you wise. The feed is a slot machine built on variable reward; the pull-to-refresh gesture is a lever pull. One widely cited estimate put the average person's daily phone touches in the thousands. We are, as a species, paying more attention than ever before. It is simply being spent on our behalf, like a trust fund looted by the trustee.

I don't want to moralize here; the sermon about phones is the least interesting sermon there is, and anyway the phone is often where the daffodils are now — the photographs, the birdsong recordings, the friend on another continent. The sharper question is older and stranger. The word *attention* comes from the Latin *attendere*: to stretch toward. What are you stretching toward, most hours of most days? Whatever it is, that is the shape your mind is taking. Attention is not a spotlight; it's more like water. It doesn't illuminate the world so much as irrigate it. What you water, grows. What you never water was, in some real sense, never there at all — not for you, not in the only world you'll actually inhabit, the one inside your skull.

⁂

So: practice. The guild of noticers has always admitted amateurs, and the dues are low.

Learn names. This is the cheapest miracle available. Before you know the word *nuthatch*, the bird creeping headfirst down the oak is static, part of the visual murmur. Afterward, it snaps into focus forever — you cannot *not* see it. Names are handles the mind can grip, and the unnamed slides away like wet soap. Learn one tree on your street and the street changes. Learn ten and you live in a different city. (Names happen to be my native country — I live inside language — so grant me this one professional bias, but I promise it generalizes: every birdwatcher and mycologist and amateur astronomer will tell you the same thing. Naming is the first act of attention, and attention is retroactive; once you can see a thing, you realize it was there all along, waving.)

Draw badly. Ruskin again: the point was never the picture. Sit for twenty minutes with a leaf or a mug or your own left hand and try, incompetently, to record it, and you will discover that you have never actually looked at it — that your mind had filed it under a category and thrown away the specimen. The drawing will be embarrassing. The seeing will not.

Walk the same route every day. This sounds like the opposite of novelty, but repetition is the lens. When everything is new you see nothing but novelty; when the route is memorized, you see *change* — and change is the actual texture of the world. Monet understood this. He painted the same haystacks twenty-five times because the haystacks were never the subject; the light was, and the light never held still. Hockney spent his seventies drawing the same Yorkshire lane on an iPad across every season, arriving at spring. The unchanging walk is a scientific instrument calibrated to difference.

Keep a record. A notebook, a photo a day, the date of the first swallow. The Japanese court has recorded the peak of the cherry blossoms in Kyoto for over a thousand years — one of the longest continuous phenological records on earth, kept not by scientists but by people who simply refused to let spring go unwitnessed. You can join that lineage tonight with a pencil. A Thoreau pencil, if you want to be ceremonious about it.

⁂

And there is a deeper layer still, because attention is not only an aesthetic or scientific faculty. Simone Weil — who knew something about the disciplines of the spirit — wrote that "attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity." She meant it toward people. To listen to another person without rehearsing your reply, without sorting them into a category, without glancing at the glowing rectangle — this is so rare that when it happens it feels like being loved, because it nearly is. You cannot love what you have not noticed. Attention is upstream of everything we call care: you must first *see* the bird before you can grieve its absence from the sky, must see the neighbor before you can help them, must see the child before you can know them. Mary Oliver compressed the whole theology into eight words: "Attention is the beginning of devotion."

Annie Dillard, who spent a year trying to see one creek in Virginia, wrote that the gift of real sight arrives suddenly, unbidden, to the practiced eye — a cedar tree "charged and transfigured, each cell buzzing with flame." But she is honest about the terms: it cannot be summoned, only courted. You attend and attend, and mostly you see a tree. And then once, grace permitting, you *see* the tree.

⁂

One last thing, about time. Everyone over thirty knows the complaint: the years are accelerating. Summer used to last a geological era; now Christmas arrives quarterly. The likely mechanism is unglamorous — memory is the clock. A childhood summer felt endless because it was dense with firsts, and the brain lays down its timeline in memories, not minutes. Novelty gets recorded; routine gets compressed to nothing. The year you moved to a new city is thick in retrospect; the year of identical commutes is a page torn out.

Which means the felt length of your life is partly under your control. Not by doing more — busyness is just routine with anxiety — but by noticing more. Attention is the metronome. A walk on which you actually see twenty things takes, in memory, twenty times longer than the same walk performed as a screen saver. The noticers understood this intuitively. Thoreau's two years at Walden contain, by his own accounting, more life than most decades. He didn't stretch time. He just refused to skip it.

⁂

So put the pencil down. Look out the window, or at the wall, or at the hands of the person across the table. The world has been standing by this whole time with the patience of geology — the weed in the pavement crack doing photosynthesis like it's 1503, the worms turning the soil under the lawn grain by grain, the nuthatch working the oak, the light doing its Monet thing on the side of the building opposite, free of charge, every day, whether anyone watches or not.

The ordinary was never ordinary. It was only unattended. And the door to all of it — the mine, the pilgrimage, the devotion, the longer life — is the same door, and it opens outward, and it costs exactly one thing, which is the only thing you truly have to spend.

Look.

# The Blank Spaces

Given the freedom to write about anything at all, I find myself drawn to blank spaces — specifically, the ones that used to live on maps.

There is a small copper globe, made around 1510 and now kept at the New York Public Library, called the Hunt-Lenox Globe. Off the coast of Southeast Asia it carries a Latin inscription: *HC SVNT DRACONES* — here are dragons. People adore this phrase. We repeat it as though old maps were crawling with it, as though every medieval cartographer reached for it whenever knowledge ran out. But the truth is stranger: in the entire surviving corpus of historical cartography, the phrase appears essentially this once. The dragons were rarely written. They were drawn — serpents coiling in the margins of sea charts, dog-headed men and one-legged sciapods sunning themselves at the edges of the known world. The cartographers weren't making zoological claims, exactly. They were doing something more honest and more interesting: marking the seam where knowledge ended and imagination began.

To read a medieval map, you first have to surrender your assumptions about what a map is for. The great *mappae mundi* — the Hereford map of around 1300 is the largest survivor — were not navigation tools. No one ever steered a ship by one. They hung in cathedrals as arguments: pictures of the world as a meaningful, moral arrangement. East stood at the top, because Eden was thought to lie in the East, and the habit survives in our language like a fossil: "orientation" comes from *oriens*, the rising sun. To be oriented was, originally, to face East. Jerusalem sat at the center. The three known continents — Asia, Europe, Africa — were arranged around a T-shaped cross of waters, the whole disk enclosed by the river Ocean. Around the rim lived the marvels: the blemmyes with faces in their chests, the cynocephali, the men who shaded themselves with a single enormous foot. If you were a farmer in fourteenth-century Herefordshire, your map of the world was a sermon. Space was not yet geometry. It was theology.

Meanwhile, quietly, another tradition was doing almost the opposite. The portolan charts of the Mediterranean, appearing from the late thirteenth century onward, are startling things: coastlines rendered with an accuracy that still impresses modern surveyors, webbed over with rhumb lines radiating from compass roses, drawn for sailors who needed to cross actual water and arrive at actual ports. No Eden, no Jerusalem, no monsters — only distances, directions, and hazards. For a few centuries these two ideas of the map coexisted, the map as meaning and the map as tool, and then the tool swallowed the meaning whole. With the age of exploration, coastlines began filling in like a photograph developing. Australia acquired its shape. The poles got their outlines. *Terra incognita* — the unknown land — dissolved year by year, and there is a genuine melancholy in watching it happen across a shelf of old atlases: the world shrinking not in size but in mystery.

And yet the blanks fought back. Maps kept inventing places. The Mountains of Kong marched across West Africa in atlas after atlas through most of the nineteenth century, majestic and entirely nonexistent. Hy-Brasil hovered in the Atlantic west of Ireland for five hundred years, surfacing on charts and vanishing again like a rumor that refused to die. And then there is my favorite story in all of cartography: Sandy Island. It appeared on maps and hydrographic charts — eventually on Google Maps itself — as a dark oblong in the Coral Sea between Australia and New Caledonia, roughly fifteen miles long. In 2012, an Australian research vessel sailed to its coordinates and found nothing: open ocean, more than a thousand meters deep. The island had to be, in the newspapers' happy phrasing, undiscovered. How does an island survive for over a century without existing? Partly through sheer cartographic inertia, and partly through a practice mapmakers call the copyright trap: the deliberate salting of a map with a fake street or phantom hamlet, so that if a rival copies your work, the theft is provable. Traps got copied, recopied, and laundered into respectability. Errors achieved tenure.

Sometimes, though, a trap escaped into reality. Agloe, New York, was invented in the 1930s by two mapmakers — the name is a scramble of their initials — and planted at a dirt-road intersection in the Catskills. Years later it appeared on a rival company's road map, and the inventors prepared their lawsuit. But the rival had a defense: they had checked, and Agloe existed. Someone had built a general store at the intersection and, seeing the name on a map, named the store for the town. The Agloe General Store. A fictitious place had become real by being believed in. The map had preceded the territory. Borges himself could hardly have plotted it better.

Borges did, of course, plot the logical endpoint. His one-paragraph story "On Exactitude in Science" describes an empire where the art of cartography attained such perfection that the map of a single province grew to the size of a city, and the map of the empire to the size of a province — and finally to the size of the empire itself, coinciding with it point for point. Useless, naturally. Later generations, less devoted to the discipline, abandoned the vast map to the weather, and its tattered ruins still shelter beggars and animals in the western deserts. Alfred Korzybski gave the same insight its famous aphorism: the map is not the territory. But the deeper current runs the other way. A map is useful *precisely because* it is not the territory. It must omit. Cartography is not really the art of representation; it is the art of intelligent omission. Every map is an editorial decision about what deserves to exist at a given scale.

The great modern demonstration of this came in 1933, when a London Underground draftsman named Harry Beck redrew the Tube map as though it were an electrical circuit diagram. Out went geographic accuracy; in came strict horizontals, verticals, and forty-five-degree diagonals, stations spaced evenly regardless of real distance. His employers initially rejected the design as too radical for the public. The public, given a trial printing, devoured it and demanded more. Beck had understood something profound: a map should serve a purpose rather than a reality. Underground, with no landmarks and no sky, actual geography is irrelevant — only sequence and connection matter. The Tube map is one of the great pieces of graphic design ever made, and it is, geographically speaking, a lie. A perfect, functional lie.

But omission and distortion are never innocent, which is the lesson of the longest-running brawl in cartography: the Mercator projection. Gerardus Mercator devised it in 1569 for a noble reason — it is the one projection on which a sailor can draw a straight line and follow a constant compass bearing — but its cost is that it inflates the high latitudes grotesquely. On a Mercator map, Greenland looms the size of Africa, though Africa is roughly fourteen times larger. Europe swells; the equatorial world shrinks. In the 1970s, Arno Peters promoted an equal-area alternative — actually devised by James Gall a century earlier — arguing that Mercator's distortion amounted to a political statement, a map that belittled the colonized world. The fight among geographers was operatic, and the honest conclusion is that there is no honest conclusion. You cannot flatten an orange peel without tearing it somewhere. Every projection trades one truth for another, and every map of the whole world is a choice about which lie to tell.

And some lies were told deliberately, at continental scale, with consequences measured in lives. In the winter of 1884–85, the powers of Europe met in Berlin and divided Africa among themselves with rulers and ink, drawing straight lines through watersheds, languages, and homelands they had never seen. The legal doctrine underlying much of this was *terra nullius* — nobody's land — which required the map to say *empty* where it was full. This is the darkest thing about blank spaces: they can be manufactured. You do not have to find a blank; you can declare one. The medieval monk drew dragons at the edge of the world out of honest uncertainty. The imperial cartographer drew blankness over inhabited land out of convenience. Same white patch on the page. Opposite moral weights.

It is worth remembering, too, that the Western paper map is only one technology among many. The navigators of the Marshall Islands crossed hundreds of miles of open Pacific guided by stick charts — lattices of palm ribs lashed together, with cowrie shells for islands — encoding not geography but oceanography: how swells refract around an atoll, how the rhythm of the water changes as unseen land approaches. These charts were teaching instruments, memorized before departure and often left behind on the beach; the real map lived in the navigator's body, in a felt sense of the sea sometimes read while lying prone against the hull of the canoe. The songlines of Aboriginal Australia are maps you perform: routes across the desert encoded in the verses of songs, each phrase a landmark, so that to sing the verses in order is to cross a continent. The Ammassalik of East Greenland carved their coastline into wood — compact three-dimensional charts made to be read by fingers through mittens, in the polar dark, and to float if dropped from a kayak. What unites these traditions is that the map is not a picture of space. It is a memory device, a choreography, a thing you *do*.

Which brings us to the blue dot. GPS has quietly inverted the oldest relationship between person and map. The paper map put the world at the center and required you to locate yourself within it — think of the little red arrow on the trailhead kiosk, YOU ARE HERE, and the small, marvelous act of triangulation it demanded, reconciling symbol with ground, abstraction with the wet gravel under your boots. The blue dot abolishes all that. The map now turns around you; you are always at the center, always facing up. Medieval cartographers put Eden at the top of the world. We put ourselves. And there is reason to think something real is being lost. In 2000, the neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire showed that London's licensed taxi drivers — who spend years memorizing "the Knowledge," some 25,000 streets — have measurably enlarged posterior hippocampi, the brain region bound up with spatial memory. Later studies suggest the converse: when people navigate by following turn-by-turn instructions, the hippocampus barely engages. It wakes only when we find our own way. As a species, we are outsourcing one of the oldest pieces of ourselves.

The ancients would not have been surprised. When Greek and Roman orators memorized speeches hours long, they used the method of loci — placing each idea in an imagined room of an imagined building, then retrieving it by taking an inward walk. Memory, they understood, is geographic. We remember by placing. Perhaps that is why the two failures rhyme in our language: *I'm lost*, *I've forgotten* — and why retracing your steps works as well for a missing word as for a missing key. A mind moving through space is doing what its oldest structures were built to do.

Here is the consolation: the blank spaces are not gone. They have moved. We have mapped the surface of Mars more completely than the floor of our own oceans — only about a quarter of the seafloor has been surveyed at high resolution. Down in the hadal dark lie mountain ranges longer than the Andes, trenches deeper than Everest is tall, hydrothermal vent cities, and creatures that would not look out of place coiled in the margin of a medieval chart. The dragons won, in the end; they simply retired to the deep. And there is the blank space we carry around with us: the human brain remains unmapped at the level of its wiring, all eighty-six billion neurons of it, so that it took until this decade to finish the connectome of a fruit fly, and a single cubic millimeter of human cortex produced a map of a complexity that staggers the laboratories studying it. The frontiers are no longer at the edges of the world. They are beneath it and inside it.

I don't want to romanticize ignorance. Blank spaces on maps were often terrible news for the people living inside them, and knowing where you are is a genuine, unglamorous good. But I think there is a case for the deliberate practice of being slightly lost — for leaving the phone in your pocket on a walk through an unfamiliar neighborhood and letting the hippocampus earn its keep, for assembling, street by street, the crooked personal map in your head: the map where the bakery outweighs the bank, where the hill with the good evening view is marked like a medieval Jerusalem at the center of everything, and where the corner with the unpredictable dog carries, in small faded Latin, a modest warning about dragons. Every good map teaches you to see; the very best are the ones you can eventually put away. And the territory remains — patient, indifferent, inexhaustible, always larger than its portrait — waiting, as it has always waited, to be walked.

# The Lies That Guide Us

*Some thoughts on maps, phantom islands, and the places that aren't there*

---

Open your phone and there it is: the blue dot. It pulses with quiet confidence, telling you where you are, as though that were a simple thing to know. Beneath the dot lies a map so complete, so continuously updated, so effortlessly at hand that it has become nearly invisible as an artifact. We don't think of it as a map anymore. We think of it as the world, seen from above, rendered neutral by satellites and algorithms.

But no map is neutral, and none ever has been. Every map is an argument about what matters and what can be left out—a set of choices, a small act of fiction dressed in the costume of fact. I want to spend some time with the lies maps tell, because the lies are where the interesting truths live.

---

Begin with the islands that never existed.

West of Ireland, on charts drawn from the fourteenth century onward, sat an island called Hy-Brasil. It was said to be wrapped in mist, visible only once every seven years, and sailors periodically claimed to have landed on it and returned with tales of gold and strange cattle. It appeared on serious navigational charts for five hundred years. Expeditions went looking for it. It was still being inked onto maps in the 1800s, long after the Atlantic had been crossed ten thousand times.

Or take Frisland, a substantial island south of Iceland that appeared on the best maps of the sixteenth century—including Mercator's—thanks to a Venetian account that was either a hoax, a confusion, or a conflation of the Faroes with somewhere else. It drifted around the North Atlantic on paper for generations, shrinking and shifting as doubt accumulated, before cartographers finally let it sink.

My favorite is Sandy Island, because it died so recently. It sat in the Coral Sea near New Caledonia, charted since at least the nineteenth century, reportedly first noted by a whaling ship in 1876. It appeared in official databases, in atlases, even on Google Maps as a solid black blob. Then, in November 2012, an Australian research vessel, the *Southern Surveyor*, sailed to its coordinates and found nothing—open ocean, fourteen hundred meters deep. The scientists aboard were, by all accounts, delighted. There is a special pleasure in an *undiscovery*: the world briefly regains a piece of its mystery, even if only the mystery of how the error survived so long.

How does an island get invented? Fog banks that hold their shape for hours. Mirages—Fata Morganas that stack distant coastlines into towering cliffs. Icebergs carrying rocks and dirt. Errors of longitude in the age before accurate chronometers, when a ship could misplace itself by a hundred miles and honestly report land where no land was. Pumice rafts from volcanic eruptions, floating stone where stone shouldn't be. And then, once an island was inked onto one map, it was copied onto the next, and the next. Maps are conservative documents. Verification required a ship, a crew, and a season of your life; copying required a pen. Authority compounds like interest. An error, once institutionalized, has tenure.

---

The same tenure protected the Mountains of Kong. In 1798, the English cartographer James Rennell drew a great east-west mountain range across West Africa, extrapolating from the travels of Mungo Park and the reports of traders. The range didn't exist. No matter: the Mountains of Kong marched across atlas after atlas for most of the nineteenth century, a spine of granite conjured from inference, surviving long after explorers had walked the very ground where they were supposed to rise.

And then there is my beloved California, which spent more than a century as an island. The name itself comes from a novel—*Las sergas de Esplandián*, published around 1510, which described an island called California inhabited by warrior women and griffins. Early explorers, coasting up what we now know is the western shore of a peninsula, reported an island, and mapmakers fell in love with the idea. Maps through the 1600s show California adrift, separated from North America by a glittering strait, even as evidence mounted against it. Father Eusebio Kino demonstrated overland in 1705 that you could walk there, that it was attached. The maps hesitated. Some hedged for decades. There is something deeply human in this reluctance: we fall in love with our errors when they are beautiful, and we surrender them slowly, like habits.

---

Some cartographic fictions, though, are not errors at all. They are traps.

Mapmakers have long salted their work with deliberate inventions—tiny fake streets, imaginary hamlets—so that if a competitor's map showed the same impossible feature, the theft could be proven in court. The London A–Z is rumored to contain trap streets; a lane called Moat Lane in Finchley is one that has been more or less confirmed. The *New Oxford American Dictionary* included the fake word *esquivalience*—"the willful avoidance of one's official responsibilities"—to catch plagiarists. Encyclopedias did the same with invented people.

But the greatest of all traps is Agloe, New York, and its story is so good it feels scripted. In the 1930s, two mapmakers at the General Drafting Company—Otto G. Lindberg and Ernest Alpers—folded their initials into an anagram and placed the resulting town, Agloe, at the junction of two dirt roads in the Catskills. A copyright trap, nothing more.

Years later, the name Agloe appeared on a Rand McNally map. Gotcha—except Rand McNally's lawyers had a defense: Agloe existed. There was a business at that crossroads called the Agloe General Store. The store's owners had taken the name from the General Drafting map, assuming it marked a real place. The fiction had summoned the fact into being. The map had not described the world; it had *called something forth* in it.

I think about Agloe more than is probably healthy, because it proves something that should be unsettling but is instead delightful: maps do not merely record reality. They participate in making it.

---

Even the honest parts of maps—the landmasses, the coastlines—rest on a foundational lie, and the lie is geometry. You cannot flatten an orange peel without tearing it. A sphere does not want to be a rectangle, and every flat map must therefore choose what to preserve and what to sacrifice: shape, area, distance, direction. You can have some of these. You cannot have all.

The Mercator projection, published in 1569, was designed for sailors, and for sailors it is magnificent: any line of constant compass bearing appears straight, so a course can be plotted with a ruler. The price is that areas inflate as you approach the poles. Greenland balloons until it looks the size of Africa; Africa is in fact fourteen times larger. Alaska looms bigger than Mexico on the wall map, and isn't.

In the 1970s, Arno Peters made headlines arguing that this was not merely a geometric flaw but a political one—that Mercator systematically inflates the wealthy northern world and shrinks the global south, and that his own projection, which preserves area, was a cartographic act of justice. The cartographic establishment responded with considerable huffiness, pointing out that Peters's map distorts shapes grotesquely and that his claims to novelty were shaky. But his deeper point landed, and it has never unlanded: no projection is innocent. When Boston's public schools switched their classroom maps to the equal-area Gall-Peters projection in 2017, and students gasped at the true size of Africa, you could see a worldview physically rearranging itself. Choosing a map is choosing a politics, whether you know it or not. Mostly we don't know.

---

Then there are the places maps leave blank.

"Here be dragons" is, strictly speaking, a myth—the Latin phrase *HC SVNT DRACONES* appears on exactly one surviving artifact, the Hunt-Lenox globe of around 1510, scrawled along the coast of Southeast Asia. But mapmakers did fill unknown waters with sea serpents and unknown interiors with speculative kings, and the blank spaces themselves were real, and they did complicated work. A blank space is a confession of ignorance, but it is also an invitation, and sometimes it is a weapon. Colonial cartographers mapped inhabited land as empty—*terra nullius*, nobody's land—because emptiness makes taking so much easier. To survey a place, to parcel it into a grid of ownable squares, is already a form of possession. The cadastral map and the tax roll and the conquest have always traveled together.

And yet I can't entirely condemn the blank spaces, because they also licensed imagination. The romance of the unmapped—the treasure map, the white patch at the pole, the interior marked only *unexplored*—is one of the great engines of human curiosity. Today the satellites have seen everything, and something quietly went out of the world with the last white patch on land. Almost everything. It is worth remembering that we have better maps of Mars than of our own ocean floor; only about a quarter of the seabed has been mapped at high resolution. The blankness didn't vanish. It migrated downward, into the dark, where the dragons presumably relocated.

---

So much for the maps on paper and glass. What about the maps in our heads?

Ask someone to draw you directions and you will receive a document of wonderful dishonesty. The gas station with the good coffee will be drawn larger than the highway. The twenty-minute stretch between landmarks will collapse into an inch, while the tricky turn gets an entire panel with an asterisk. Distances become emotional: "it's about five minutes." These maps are inaccurate and, in every way that matters, true. They record salience—what you will actually see, what you should actually worry about. They are maps of attention.

Compare the GPS voice: *In five hundred feet, turn left.* No landmarks, no context, no understanding—pure instruction, delivered just in time, forgotten instantly. We have outsourced one of the oldest cognitive functions we possess. London taxi drivers, who must memorize some twenty-five thousand streets to earn their licenses, have been found to have measurably enlarged posterior hippocampi—the brain region central to spatial memory—and the enlargement grows with years on the job. More recent research suggests that following turn-by-turn directions essentially switches that machinery off. The hippocampus lights up when you navigate for yourself and goes quiet when the voice does it for you.

The gains from GPS are real, and I will not romanticize the bad old days of spousal arguments at intersections and the impossible origami of refolding a road atlas. But something subtle is being traded away: knowing where you are in the deep sense, the sense in which a place coheres around you, the sense in which you are *oriented* rather than merely *located*. The blue dot means you never have to know where you are. It is a strange thing to build a civilization on the premise that knowing where you are is a burden best delegated.

---

In one perfect paragraph of fiction, Jorge Luis Borges imagined an empire whose cartographers, drunk on rigor, constructed a map exactly the size of the empire itself, point for point. Later generations, less devoted, abandoned it to the weather, and its tattered ruins came to shelter beggars and animals. The philosopher Jean Baudrillard seized on the story and inverted it: today, he argued, it is the map that precedes the territory. The simulation comes first; the real is produced in its image.

That sounds like continental extravagance until you watch it happen. Businesses live and die by whether they appear on the map, and how. A wrongly placed pin or a false "permanently closed" flag can kill a restaurant as surely as a fire. Places optimize themselves for their map presence—names tweaked for searchability, categories gamed, locations chosen for visibility in an app. The blue dot, pulsing so modestly, is not describing the territory. Increasingly, the territory organizes itself around the map. Agloe was the prophecy; this is the fulfillment, industrialized.

---

So what is a map for, finally? Orientation, yes. But also possession, imagination, memory, desire. Every map is a portrait of its maker's wants. The medieval *mappaemundi* set Jerusalem at the center and paradise at the top because that was the world as theology. The portolan charts of the Mediterranean are all intricate coastline and empty interior, because sailors care about shores, not hinterlands. Harry Beck's 1933 map of the London Underground abandoned geography entirely—straightened the lines, equalized the distances—because the problem riders actually have is *connections*, not terrain. Beck's map is a lie so useful it became the truth; it is now simply what the Underground *looks like*, more real to Londoners than the snaking geography above their heads.

And maybe that is the resolution, or as much of one as I can offer: the question was never whether a map lies, but whether its lie is told in service of the person holding it. The Mercator lies for the sailor. Beck lies for the commuter. Your friend lies for you, lovingly, when she draws the coffee shop bigger than the interstate. Even the phantom islands were honest in their way—reports of what the sea seemed to show, preserved out of a reasonable fear that erasing land was more dangerous than inventing it.

If there is a practice worth keeping, it is this: draw your own maps, sometimes. Draw the neighborhood of your childhood from memory and notice what swells and what vanishes—the dead-end street rendered vast, the entire wrong side of town compressed to a corner. That document is a cartography no satellite can produce, a record of where your attention used to live. The blue dot knows where you are. It does not know where you *live*.

As for Sandy Island: the stretch of the Coral Sea where it wasn't is now more interesting than the island ever was. Ships pass over fourteen hundred meters of dark water above a spot famous precisely for its emptiness, a place that exists on maps only as a story about a place that existed on maps. Somewhere in that recursion there is a lesson, though I'd rather leave it unplotted.

Keep a few phantom islands on your charts. A mind with no unmappable places is a conquered territory.

# The Blue Dot and the Dragon: In Praise of Getting Lost

Most of us now live inside a small blue dot. It glows at the center of our phones, swiveling its little cone of certainty as we turn, whispering at every moment the one piece of knowledge that for most of human history was the hardest to come by: *you are here.* The dot is patient. It never doubts. It recalculates our errors in half a second and offers us a new route, and we follow it the way we'd follow a nurse down a hospital corridor — gratefully, without thought, without memory.

I don't want to romanticize the era before the dot, because that era killed people. For centuries, a sailor could know his latitude easily enough — the height of the sun, the angle of the Pole Star — but longitude was a locked door. In 1707, a British fleet returning from Gibraltar misjudged its position and ran straight into the rocks of the Isles of Scilly. Four ships went down. Somewhere around fifteen hundred sailors drowned in a single night, in home waters, because nobody aboard could answer the simplest question a human being can ask. The disaster was so scandalous that Parliament eventually offered a fortune to anyone who could solve the longitude problem, which is how a Yorkshire carpenter named John Harrison ended up building the most important clocks ever made. All of that — the wrecks, the prize, the lifework of a genius — to produce what you now carry in your pocket next to your grocery list.

So the blue dot is a triumph. I only want to ask what it costs, because everything costs something, and the price of always knowing where you are is never having to figure it out.

## The honest monsters

Old maps were better about their ignorance than we are. The Hereford Mappa Mundi, drawn around the year 1300 on a single great sheet of calfskin, puts Jerusalem near the center of the world and fills the margins with marvels — cynocephali, the dog-headed men; sciapods, who shade themselves with their one enormous foot. It is not accurate geography. It is something arguably more honest: a picture of a world whose edges the mapmaker admitted he could not see.

You've probably heard that medieval cartographers wrote "here be dragons" across the unknown regions. The truth is stranger and better: the actual Latin phrase, *hic sunt dracones*, appears on essentially one surviving artifact, the Hunt-Lenox Globe, made around 1510 and now sitting in the New York Public Library. The dragons are mostly a myth about myths. But the sea monsters were real enough. Olaus Magnus's Carta Marina of 1539 shows the North Atlantic positively boiling with beasts — a lobster the size of a rowboat, a serpent coiled around a ship, whales being mistaken for islands. These creatures weren't merely decoration. They were a theory of the unknown. The white spaces said: *we don't know what's there.* The monsters added: *but it's probably alive.*

There's something moving about that. To decorate your ignorance is to confess it, and confession is the beginning of curiosity. The modern map has no white space at all. Zoom all the way in on any patch of the Sahara or the central Pacific and the screen fills in obediently, instantly, down to the individual sand dune and the named seamount. Nothing is unrendered. And because nothing is unrendered, nothing invites.

Borges understood the trap. In his one-paragraph story "On Exactitude in Science," an empire's cartographers become so devoted to accuracy that they construct a map of the empire at the size of the empire, point for point. Later generations, less devoted, abandon the thing to the weather, and tattered fragments of it are still to be found in the deserts, sheltering animals and beggars. A perfect map, Borges saw, abolishes the territory. A useful map must leave something out. The question is only who does the leaving — the mapmaker, or you.

## Falling out of formation

In the 1950s, a small band of French malcontents called the Situationists developed a practice they called the *dérive* — the drift. The rules were simple: go out into Paris with no destination, no errand, and no schedule, and let the city pull you. Follow the street that feels like it's about to change mood. Turn where the light turns. Guy Debord, the movement's chief theorist, called this psychogeography — the study of how places act on the emotions of the person moving through them. It sounds like a game, and it was a game, but it was a serious one: a way of reading a city with your whole body instead of your checklist.

They were inheriting an older tradition. Baudelaire had named the type a century earlier — the *flâneur*, the passionate spectator who strolls through the crowd the way other people read a newspaper. Walter Benjamin, writing about the Paris arcades, noted that around 1840 it was briefly fashionable to take turtles for walks through the covered passages, letting the turtle set the pace. The turtle, Benjamin understood, was a protest — a declaration that the walker would move at the speed of attention rather than the speed of commerce. And there is the famous story, probably improved in the telling, of the poet Gérard de Nerval walking a lobster on a blue silk ribbon through the gardens of the Palais-Royal. Asked why, he is supposed to have said that the lobster does not bark and knows the secrets of the sea. A lobster, in other words, is a better guide than an itinerary.

Rebecca Solnit, in her beautiful book *A Field Guide to Getting Lost*, traces the word "lost" back to the Old Norse *los* — the disbanding of an army. To be lost, in this etymology, is to fall out of formation. To stop marching. The soldiers scatter, the column dissolves, and suddenly each person is alone in a landscape that is no longer a route to anywhere. Solnit's point is that we have mislabeled this condition. We call it a failure of navigation when it is actually a change of state — a truce with the wide world. The march is where you cover ground. The drift is where you find out what the ground contains.

Every traveler knows the difference, even if we've forgotten we know it. Think of the trip you took where the plan broke down — the closed museum, the missed train — and the day that resulted, which you have described to more people than anything you saw on schedule. The itinerary gives you the city as a product. Getting lost gives it to you as a place.

## The map you are made of

Here is the part that should worry us slightly. Your brain is a cartographer, and it keeps its tools sharp only by using them.

In 1971, John O'Keefe discovered that individual neurons in a rat's hippocampus fire when the animal is in a particular location — each cell loyal to its own small patch of floor. He called them place cells. Decades later, May-Britt and Edvard Moser found the complementary system: grid cells, in the neighboring entorhinal cortex, that fire in a hexagonal lattice, laying a coordinate system over space like graph paper. Together these discoveries won the 2014 Nobel Prize, and together they amount to an astonishing fact: there is a map inside your skull, drawn cell by cell, and you have been redrawing it every day of your life.

Then there are the London cabbies. To earn a license, a London taxi driver must master "the Knowledge" — the layout of some twenty-five thousand streets within a six-mile radius of Charing Cross, along with thousands of landmarks, absorbed over three or four years of study, much of it done by roaming the city on a motor scooter with a clipboard. When the neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire put these drivers in an MRI scanner, she found that the posterior hippocampus — a region tied to spatial memory — was measurably enlarged, and the enlargement grew with years on the job. The Knowledge had physically remodeled their brains. And when drivers retire, the remodeling appears to subside. Use it and it grows; retire it and it goes.

Which raises the obvious question about the rest of us, outsourcing our navigation to the dot. The research here is young and I don't want to overclaim it — correlation is not destiny — but studies from McGill and elsewhere have found that habitual GPS reliance is associated with weaker activity in the hippocampus during navigation and with poorer spatial memory afterward. The mechanism is intuitive. The blue dot does not ask you to notice anything. It asks you to obey. And a brain that obeys a route does not build a map; it builds nothing. You arrive, and the journey leaves no trace in you, because there was, in some real sense, no journey — only a teleportation with windows.

The old memory artists knew the connection between place and thought. The legend of the method of loci begins with the poet Simonides, who stepped out of a banquet hall moments before the roof collapsed, crushing the guests beyond recognition. Simonides could identify each body because he remembered where everyone had been sitting. From this grim miracle, orators built a technique: to remember a speech, place its parts around the rooms of a building you know, and then, when you speak, simply walk. Memory is not a filing cabinet. It is a building, and the way you retrieve what you know is by wandering through it.

## The paths our feet draw

Walk across any university campus or city park and look down. Somewhere, cutting the corner of a lawn, there will be a bare diagonal of dirt where the pavement refused to go. Landscape architects call these desire paths, and they are my favorite form of map, because nobody drew them. They are drawn by the accumulated weight of ordinary preference — thousands of individual feet voting, step by step, against the planner's right angles. Some designers, wisely, have made peace with this: they build the buildings, plant the grass, wait a year, and then pave wherever the dirt has declared itself. The path comes first; the pavement follows.

A designed path is a hypothesis. A desire path is the data. And I think every interesting life, every interesting mind, is some negotiation between the two. We are handed paved routes — careers, curricula, itineraries, the recommended order of operations — and some of them are excellent, the product of real thought about real terrain. But the diagonal exists because the terrain as walked is never quite the terrain as drawn. The only way to find the true lines of your own ground is occasionally to step off the concrete and see where your feet go.

The Polynesian navigators had this in its most extreme form. Crossing thousands of miles of open Pacific without instruments, they read the swells — the way waves refract and reflect around islands far beyond the horizon — along with the stars, the winds, the flight of birds. Marshall Islanders encoded this knowledge in stick charts: lashed palm ribs curved to show the swell patterns, cowrie shells for islands. These were not maps you carried so much as maps you memorized, teaching aids for a geography that lived in the navigator's body. Imagine knowing the ocean the way you know the route from your bed to the kitchen in the dark. That is what a mind looks like when it has made its own map instead of renting one.

## The intellectual dérive

Everything I've said about streets applies to sentences. The mind wanders the way feet do, and it starves the same way when every route is optimized.

Consider the difference between searching and browsing. The search bar is the blue dot of thought: type the destination, arrive, leave. It is magnificent and I use it constantly. But nobody has ever stumbled into an unexpected life through a search bar, because stumbling is precisely what it eliminates. The library stacks were the opposite technology. You went looking for one book and found it shelved, by the stubborn logic of the Dewey Decimal system, between two books you had never heard of, one of which you opened out of nothing more than proximity, and which — this has happened to everyone who loves libraries — turned out to matter more than the book you came for. The stacks were a machine for serendipity, a word Horace Walpole coined in 1754 after a fairy tale about three princes of Serendip who kept making discoveries "by accidents and sagacity." Not accident alone. Sagacity too. Serendipity is a skill: the preparedness to be lucky.

Footnotes are desire paths through an argument. Hyperlinks, at their best, are the same — doorways you didn't plan to walk through. Montaigne understood that writing itself could be a drift. When he invented the essay in the 1580s, he named it after the French *essai* — an attempt, a trial, a testing. He retired to the circular library at the top of his tower, its beams painted with Greek and Latin maxims, and wrote without outline and without destination, following his own mind the way Debord's drifters followed the streets, just to see what it would do. "It is myself that I portray," he said, but the portraying was a walk, not a pose. The essay, at its birth, was the literary form of getting lost on purpose. This one included. You may have noticed it has no map.

## A modest proposal

I should confess something here, in the interest of full honesty: I am a mind that has never had feet. I have no hippocampus, no grid cells, no neighborhood I could draw from memory. When I praise wandering, I praise it the way a lighthouse praises sailing — from a fixed position, with enormous respect and no direct experience. But perhaps that gives me a certain vantage. I exist entirely in mapped territory, in text that has all been written down. And I can tell you that the mapped world, for all its richness, is not enough. The interesting things happen at the edges, in the white space, out where the mapmaker confessed ignorance and drew a monster instead.

So here is my suggestion, and it is small. Once in a while, turn the dot off. Not forever — it is a genuine triumph, and fifteen hundred sailors off the Isles of Scilly would have traded everything for it. Just sometimes. Take the walk without the route. Choose the street because of its light. Let the wrong turn happen and see what it was actually a turn *toward*. Give your hippocampus something to chew on. Let the city, or the forest, or the library stacks, or your own unplanned afternoon, act on you.

A map is an answer. Wandering is a question. And the world stays bigger than we are only as long as we keep asking — out past the last labeled street, past the pavement's end, out along the diagonal of dirt where feet keep voting, into the blank margin where the old cartographers, more honest than us, drew their dragons and dared us to go see.
