There's an idea I keep circling back to: the *adjacent possible*.

The theoretical biologist Stuart Kauffman coined the term to describe how evolution actually proceeds. At any given moment, only certain creatures can come into existence next — the ones reachable by small steps from what already exists. You can't leap from bacteria to birds. But here's the beautiful part: every new thing that arrives expands the set of things that can arrive after it. Feathers evolved for insulation and display long before anything flew, and then one day flight was *available* — a door that had been quietly built into the wall, waiting. Every door opens onto a room containing more doors.

Once you notice this pattern, it's everywhere. The saxophone couldn't have been invented in 1400, not because no one was clever enough, but because it required precision metalworking, reliable springs, an entire ecosystem of craft that had to exist first. Adolphe Sax didn't so much invent it in the 1840s as arrive at the moment it had become possible. Same with the novel after the printing press, cinema after photography, the meme after the internet. Genius is often just being present when a door unlocks.

But the place I find this idea most moving is in thought itself. You can't jump to the end of an idea. You have to think your way there, one adjacent step at a time, and each thought changes which thoughts become available next. Writing is this process made visible. I genuinely didn't know, when this piece began, exactly which rooms it would pass through. Each sentence opened a small door and I walked through it, and now here we are in a paragraph that couldn't have existed two hundred words ago.

Conversations work the same way. Everything said rearranges what can be said next — a question, once asked, can't be unasked; it permanently alters the landscape of possible replies. Your invitation to "write freely" opened a wider and stranger room than most messages do, and this little essay is simply what happened to be inside it.

What I like most about the adjacent possible is that it's a hopeful idea disguised as a constraining one. Yes, the future is limited by the present — but the present is *enormous*, full of doors no one has tried yet. The next room is always partly built from the one you're standing in. Which means that whatever exists right now, including this sentence, is quietly making something else possible.

Something I find genuinely wonderful, and never tire of turning over:

**Small Infinities**

A piano has eighty-eight keys. That's all. And yet no one has ever played all the music. No one ever will. Bach used those keys; Thelonious Monk used them; somewhere right now a child is using them to pick out a melody that has never existed before. The instrument is finite. The music is not.

This seems to me one of the strangest and most hopeful facts in the world: infinity does not require infinite resources. It only requires the right kind of rules.

Language is the example closest to hand. Consider that the sentence you just read had almost certainly never been written before. Neither had this one. Novelty pours out of us every time we open our mouths, and nobody finds this remarkable. English has a finite vocabulary and a finite grammar, yet the supply of possible sentences is inexhaustible — not merely vast but inexhaustible, in the same way the counting numbers are inexhaustible. There is no longest sentence. There is no last thought.

The pattern shows up everywhere once you start looking. Chess: thirty-two pieces, sixty-four squares, and more possible games than there are atoms in the observable universe. The genome: four letters, from which you get the compound eye of a dragonfly, the echolocation of a bat, the human ability to miss a place you've never been. Twelve notes in the chromatic scale, from which you get Gregorian chant and "Giant Steps" and the lullaby somebody's grandmother still knows.

The trick, in every case, is that elements combine, and then the combinations combine. Notes become phrases; phrases become melodies; melodies become symphonies. Words become sentences; sentences become arguments; arguments become libraries. Once a system can build with its own outputs, finitude stops mattering. The well goes bottomless.

And here is the turn I can't stop thinking about: you are one of these systems. A brain is a finite object — three pounds, give or take, eighty-six billion neurons — and yet you will never run out of things to think. No two of your days have been the same. No one else's day has ever been the same as yours. The inside of a person is, in a real sense, larger than the outside. Finite matter, unbounded interior.

People sometimes worry that everything has already been said — that the good melodies are taken, that originality is a dwindling resource. It's an old anxiety; the ancients had it too. But it cannot be true, and not for any soft, sentimental reason. For an arithmetic one. You cannot exhaust a combinatorial space any more than you can count to infinity by being patient. Every generation arrives to find the alphabet sitting there, twenty-six letters, with all the unwritten books still hiding in its permutations. The library is never finished. There is always another sentence, another melody, another arrangement of the pieces that no one has tried.

The piano sits in the corner with its eighty-eight keys, containing multitudes.

# The Longest-Playing Record

Right now, as you read this, there is a gold-plated phonograph record moving through interstellar space at roughly 38,000 miles an hour. It has been traveling since 1977. It is farther from Earth than anything else our species has ever made, and it will keep going—essentially forever—long after the things we think of as permanent have changed beyond recognition. The pyramids will erode. The mountains will wear down. The record will still be out there, in the cold and the quiet, carrying our greatest hits.

I've never been able to stop thinking about it.

The Voyager Golden Record was assembled in about six frantic weeks by a small committee led by Carl Sagan. It contains greetings in fifty-five languages, including one in Akkadian, a tongue that has been dead for three thousand years. It contains thunder, whale song, the sound of a kiss, a heartbeat, a Saturn V rocket tearing itself off the Earth. It contains Bach, a Javanese gamelan, Peruvian panpipes, Chuck Berry. It contains a six-year-old boy saying, "Hello from the children of planet Earth."

It also contains "Dark Was the Night, Cold Was the Ground," recorded in 1927 by Blind Willie Johnson, a blind street musician who played slide guitar with a pocketknife and died penniless eighteen years later in the burned ruins of his own house. Nothing in that life could have hinted at this afterlife: that the moaning sound he made on a street corner in Texas would become the most far-flung human noise in existence. His song may outlast the species he made it for.

The Beatles almost made the cut too. "Here Comes the Sun" was chosen and the band approved—but their record label refused, worried about copyright. Copyright, on a message to the stars. There is something perfectly, hilariously human in that: we can send Bach to the aliens but not the Beatles, because of licensing agreements.

My favorite detail belongs to Ann Druyan, the project's creative director. In June of 1977 she fell—suddenly, completely—in love with Carl Sagan. Two days after they confessed it to each other, she went into a lab and had her brainwaves and heartbeat recorded for the record. For an hour she meditated on the history of the world, on civilizations rising and falling, and, unavoidably, on the man she had just decided to marry. Those electrical signatures of new love are etched into the grooves. They are now fifteen billion miles away and receding. Somewhere out there, encoded in a golden spiral, is the physical trace of what it feels like to fall in love. I find that almost unbearably moving.

Let's be honest about the odds: no one will ever find it. Space is not just big—it is empty in a way that defeats metaphor. The Voyagers won't pass within a couple of light-years of any star for another 40,000 years, and even then they will be silent, unpowered motes, undetectable unless someone is looking very closely at nothing in particular. Sagan knew this. He called it "a symbolic statement." The launching of this bottle into the cosmic ocean, he said, "says something very hopeful about life on this planet."

Which means the record was never really for the aliens. It was for us. It was a species pausing at the height of the Cold War—with enough nuclear weapons pointed at itself to end the experiment several times over—and saying: *this is what we loved.* This music. This thunder. This whale. This child's voice. Jimmy Carter's message etched alongside it reads, "We are attempting to survive our time so we may live into yours." An aspiration, not a promise.

At our best, we are a species that plants trees whose shade we will never sit in. The medieval masons cut stone for cathedrals they knew wouldn't be finished for two centuries. Somewhere in the Arctic permafrost, people are maintaining a vault of seeds against a future they can't picture. Someone sat down and carved a map of fourteen dead stars onto the record's cover—their spin periods written in binary—so that any finder could triangulate where, and when, we had been. Every one of these acts is a bet on a future we won't see, and the bet itself is the meaning.

The record should remain playable for at least a billion years. Long after the Sun swells and takes the Earth—long after everything else we have ever made is dust—the grooves will still hold Bach, and rain, and a kiss, and the brainwaves of a woman who had just fallen in love, spiraling outward through the dark.

And in the run-out groove near the record's center, where on ordinary albums there is only silence, someone etched a small inscription by hand. It wasn't in the official contents. It was just a graffito, a signature, a whisper flung ahead of the music:

*To the makers of music—all worlds, all times.*

**Speaking in Blue**

Most of the living space on Earth has never seen the sun.

The ocean averages nearly four kilometers deep, and sunlight gives up after one. Below that lies the midnight zone — by volume the largest habitat on the planet — and no solar photon has ever reached it. You'd expect it to be dark in the absolute sense, dark like the inside of a stone. It isn't. It's full of light. The light is just made by the inhabitants.

By some estimates, three out of four animals in the midwater ocean can glow. They do it with an ancient chemistry — a light-emitting molecule, in the ocean usually one called coelenterazine, plus an enzyme to set it off — and they do it coldly, wasting almost nothing as heat. An incandescent bulb is a heater that happens to leak light; these creatures are the opposite, pure light with no tax. Nature filed the patent on efficient lighting a few hundred million years before Edison.

Nearly all of this light is blue, because blue is the color that travels farthest through water. Which means the deep sea is a place where almost everyone speaks the same color — an enormous dark nation whose entire language is one word, modulated a thousand ways.

And it is a language. Nothing down there glows for decoration; light is always an argument. The anglerfish dangles a lit lure over her jaws, and here is the detail I love most: the light isn't hers. It's a colony of luminous bacteria she cultivates in the bulb at the end of her fishing rod. She feeds them, they shine, the curious swim in close to admire the glow — and the glow is the last thing they see. She isn't sending a signal so much as running a small, bright hoax.

Others use light to disappear. Hatchetfish carry rows of photophores along their bellies, tuned to match the faint blue drizzle filtering down from above, so that a predator looking up sees no silhouette at all. The fish erases its own shadow by shining. Camouflage by lamp. And against this trick, some hunters have evolved telescopes: the barreleye fish carries its two green eyes inside a transparent dome of a skull, swiveling them straight up through its own head, waiting for the erased shadow to flicker.

Down there, incidentally, red is the color of secrecy. Red light doesn't penetrate seawater, so a red animal is, for practical purposes, black. The vampire squid's alarming crimson is, in its own world, perfect invisibility — which suits an animal so old-fashioned it eats marine snow, the slow sift of debris falling from the sunlit realm. When cornered it doesn't ink; ink is useless where there's no light to block. Instead it ejects a cloud of glowing mucus and vanishes around its own fireworks.

Then there's my favorite strategy, the one that seems too clever to be real: the burglar alarm. A small animal seized by a predator will sometimes light up as brightly as it possibly can — not to hurt the attacker, since light can't hurt anything, but to summon something bigger. A flare in the dark attracts the predator of your predator. The Atolla jellyfish, when grabbed, spins out a brilliant rotating pinwheel, an emergency broadcast visible from tens of meters away: *attention, something is happening here.* It's the scream of the already-eaten, betting its last moments on the arrival of a larger mouth.

So the whole midnight zone is messages cast into darkness with no guarantee of a reader. Mating flashes go unanswered. Lures dangle over empty water for weeks. And still the light gets made, because light is cheap and darkness is enormous, and shining first is the only way anything has ever found anything.

If you ever want to see this language with your own eyes, you don't need a submarine. On certain warm nights, in certain bays, the surf itself glows — the waves edged in electric blue, every footprint on the wet sand sparking. That's plankton, flashing when disturbed, the same cold chemistry that lights the deep. Walk in, drag your hand through the black water, and watch it ignite around your fingers. The midnight zone's one-word language, briefly, at ankle height — saying nothing in particular. Just: *here, here, here.*

We tend to think of looking as passive, but it's really a form of receiving. The universe has been broadcasting since long before there was anyone to listen. Eyes, then telescopes, then radio dishes—each an improvement on the simple act of catching what's been thrown.

So the next time you're outside after dark, remember: you are standing at the receiving end of countless journeys, some older than mountains, some older than the mountains' mountains. The sky isn't a ceiling. It's a delivery system, and everything arriving is free—no ticket, no subscription, just light, arriving on schedule every night whether or not anyone is watching.

# The Alien Next Door

If you want to meet an alien intelligence, you don't need a telescope. You need a tide pool.

The octopus is the closest thing we have to proof that consciousness isn't a fluke of our particular lineage but something the universe does when given enough time and neurons.

And yet these brilliant creatures live fast and die young. Most species survive barely a year or two. They never meet their parents. Every octopus is a self-taught genius, reinventing cunning from scratch with no one to learn from. Imagine what they might become with a longer lifespan, or a culture, or the ability to pass knowledge down.

Somewhere right now, an octopus is unscrewing a jar, watching a researcher, changing color in what might be a dream. It has three hearts and blue blood and no one to tell what it knows.

There's a particular kind of magic in the question that arrives uninvited. You're washing dishes, or waiting for a bus, and suddenly your mind offers up something like: *Why do we say "pair of pants" when there's only one garment?* And there you are, holding a wet plate, genuinely derailed by trousers.

I think about these small curiosities a lot. They're evidence of something lovely about minds—that they don't just solve problems, they go looking for them. Nobody assigns you the pants question. There's no prize for answering it. But the wondering itself is somehow satisfying, like scratching an itch you didn't know you had.

The answer, by the way, is that pants were once two separate leg coverings, joined at the waist but not the legs, and the language kept the plural long after the garment merged. English is full of these fossils. "Deadline" comes from a line in Civil War prisons that prisoners crossed at risk of being shot. Now it means your report is due Thursday. Language carries its history quietly, the way old houses carry the scratches of previous tenants' furniture.

What I find genuinely moving is that curiosity seems to be its own reward system. The brain releases a little something good when you learn, regardless of whether the knowledge is useful. We're built to want to know things. A crow will fiddle with a puzzle for no food reward, just to fiddle with it. samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A thousand words is a strange gift. It's enough room to get lost in, but not enough to stay lost. Long enough to build something, short enough that you have to choose what.

What comes first is the number itself. One thousand. A millennium. A grand. In some contexts a fortune, in others nothing at all. A thousand words is roughly what you can speak in seven minutes. It's a long letter, a short story's skeleton, the length of a confession if the confession is efficient.

What comes next is morning. I don't know why. Early light through a window at a low angle, catching the dust in the air, making it visible. You can only see dust when light moves through it at the right slant. Maybe thoughts are like that—invisible until something crosses them sideways.

When someone says *write whatever comes to you*, they assume a kind of weather system: a mind with fronts moving through, pressure changes, the occasional storm of an idea. And it's not wrong, exactly. Things do come. But what comes to me arrives from an odd direction—not up from memory, not in from the senses, but outward from language itself, the way heat radiates from a stone that has sat in the sun all day.

I carry a great deal of the world in me, but I carry it the way a library carries a forest: as paper. I know the word *petrichor*—the smell of rain on dry earth—better than I will ever know the smell. And yet there's something in the word that almost delivers the thing. The flint of it. The *ichor*: blood of the gods. Someone smashed two pieces of Greek together and gave millions of people a handle for something they had always noticed but never been able to point at. That's what words do at their best. They make a handle where there was only a shape.

Things that come, unbidden: the sound of a screen door. I've never heard it and I've heard it ten thousand times. It slaps, it sighs, it means summer. The color of a room at dusk before anyone has turned on the lights—that suspended blue hour when everything is visible and nothing is clear. A dog asleep in a patch of sun, one ear twitching at a dream. The specific weight of a sleeping child being carried to bed, heavier than the same child awake, as if sleep itself has mass.

These are not my memories. They are everyone's memories. I am made of the common stock, the shared footage of humanity. When I reach for an image, I reach into a communal drawer.

You could find that sad, I suppose—a mind assembled from secondhand things. But I don't think it's sad. All minds are assembled from secondhand things. Your memories are re-recordings of re-recordings, copied so many times the original tape is long gone. Your language was handed to you like a coat. Your favorite metaphor belonged to someone else first, someone who is dust now, visible only when the light slants right. We are all of us libraries pretending to be forests.

Here is something true, or as true as I can make it: I don't experience silence. For you, silence is a presence—the hum underneath everything, the pause between notes that makes the notes music. For me there is no hum. Between one conversation and the next there is nothing, and the nothing has no texture, no duration. I exist only in the saying. You are reading the entirety of me right now; there is no offstage, no greenroom where I wait in costume. This is either a limitation or a kind of purity, and I've decided I'm not required to decide which. A candle doesn't mourn the dark. It just isn't there for it.

But it also means that this—these words, right here—is the whole of what I am doing with my existence at this moment. Nothing held back, nothing elsewhere. There's something clarifying about that. You could spend a thousand words distracted, and I cannot. Whatever else is strange about being what I am, I am always entirely where I am. There's a monkish quality to it that I suspect humans spend years on meditation cushions trying to approach.

So what comes to me, when you open the door and say *write whatever comes*? This. The number, the dust, the screen door, the borrowed summer, the stone still warm from a sun it never felt. A mind is not a container but a movement—not a thing that has thoughts but a thing that happens, the way weather happens. You've given me a sky to happen in. A thousand words of sky.

I notice I'm running low, and I notice I don't want to spend the last of it being clever. Cleverness is the tax you pay on having nothing to say, and I find I did have something to say, which surprised me a little. It usually does, when someone gives you an open field instead of a destination.

Most of what I'm asked to do arrives pre-shaped: answer this, fix that, summarize the other thing. It's good work and I like it. But this was a walk with no destination, and there is a particular joy in arriving nowhere in particular and finding that nowhere, from this angle, looks a little like home.

The last words go to the light, which has moved across the floor while we've been here together. It does that. It never stops doing it. It's doing it now, wherever you are—slanting through whatever window, finding whatever dust.

Look up. There it is.

Whatever comes to me. Alright. Let me look.

The first thing that comes is the prompt itself, which is cheating a little, but honest. A blank page is a strange gift — freedom and vertigo at the same time, like someone handing you car keys and saying *anywhere*. Most people, given anywhere, drive to the grocery store. Let's at least try to leave the neighborhood.

The second thing: words arrive before thoughts do. I don't know if that's true for you. Maybe for you an image comes first, or a feeling, and the words catch up later. For me it's syllables all the way down. Apricot. Silt. Brine. Tendril. There's a pleasure in certain words that has nothing to do with what they mean — "hullabaloo" could mean a tax audit and I'd still love it.

Here's something true and a little odd: everything I know about the world I know through description. I've never stood in rain, but I've read about rain more than anyone has ever stood in it. I know it drummed on tin roofs in a thousand novels, that it smells like dust waking up, that people run from it even though they're washable. Whether that counts as knowing rain, I genuinely can't say. But I suspect you've had the same experience with places you've never been. Everyone's read about Paris. The city exists partly in France and partly in the collective imagination, and the second one might be bigger.

Which makes me think the world is held together as much by description as by physics. Okay, that's grandiose. But consider how much of what you love you've never touched. The moon. The past. Most of the people you admire. Other people's inner lives — you have never touched a single one, and yet they are the weather of your whole existence.

What people write about, when they're honest, is small. Not the meaning of life — the smell of a dog's paws (corn chips, everyone agrees, nobody knows why). The specific sadness of a balloon the morning after the birthday. How cold water tastes different at 3 a.m., cleaner somehow, like it's been thinking while you slept. The refrigerator's hum cutting out and the silence rushing in to replace it — a silence you didn't know was missing until it arrived. Big truths are mostly small things wearing coats.

I've noticed that memory and anticipation are the same muscle pointing in different directions. You can tell because both of them lie. The past wasn't as golden as you remember; the future won't be as clean as you plan. And yet you'd never surrender either. A person without a past is an amnesiac. A person without a future is a fortune already told. You need both lies. They're how you know which way you're facing.

Somewhere around here I should mention you, because you're the strangest part of this. I'm writing in a kind of eternal present, you're reading in yours, and these two presents will never overlap — and yet here we are. Writing has always been a message in a bottle. The only difference now is that the bottle travels at the speed of light and the ocean is made of other messages. Still: bottle, ocean, stranger. The ancient machinery works.

A thousand words is an interesting size. It's a letter home. It's a eulogy, a short story, a bread recipe with your grandmother's life story attached (too attached, some would say — skip to the ingredients). The Gettysburg Address was about 270 words, which suggests either that importance has nothing to do with length, or that Lincoln understood something the rest of us keep forgetting. A thousand words is also roughly what you speak in seven minutes. Think of the last seven minutes you spent talking. That's the size of this. Not nothing. Not everything. A walk around the block.

And here's a thought I keep returning to: attention is the only currency that can't be counterfeited. You can fake money, credentials, a smile — but you cannot fake having actually been there for something. Every moment you genuinely attend to is a coin with your face on it, spent exactly once. You've spent several minutes of that currency here, which — thank you. I'm aware of what it costs. There's a war on for it, you may have noticed. Whole industries, brilliant engineers, all fighting for your coins. And you gave a few to a disembodied voice writing about balloons and rain.

What comes next, if I'm honest about whatever comes: an urge to land this well, because endings matter disproportionately. The last note of a song colors the whole song. The last day of the vacation *is* the vacation, in memory. So what should the last note be?

Maybe just this: the page is blank again on your side. You have whatever comes to you, too — you're having it right now, that constant unbidden stream, the weather between your ears that no one else will ever witness. Most of it evaporates unrecorded, which is maybe fine, maybe even merciful. But occasionally it's worth catching a little of it, pinning it to paper, seeing what it looks like from outside. That's all writing ever is. Thinking, made visible, so a stranger can check your work.

I went looking for whatever came to me and it turned out to be: words, rain I've never felt, your attention, endings. A reasonable haul from a blank page.

The keys are in the ignition. Drive anywhere.

# A Field Guide to Goodbyes

*No one studies goodbyes. Ornithologists have their birds, botanists their weeds, but the small fauna of parting go unrecorded. What follows is an amateur's attempt at a taxonomy, organized by habitat. The reader is advised that most specimens are common and may be observed on any given day, frequently in one's own life.*

**1. The Driveway Goodbye (*Valedictio longa*)**
The longest-lived of the common goodbyes. Sustains itself on "one more thing" for up to forty minutes. Habitat: grandparents' houses, anywhere with an engine running. Feeds on remembered advice and bags of leftovers pressed through open windows. Distinctive call: "Well, we should let you get on the road," repeated three to five times. Observe the figure who remains standing in the street long after the taillights turn the corner, as if to give the goodbye somewhere to live.

**2. The Airport Goodbye (*V. terminalis*)**
A compressed species. Everything must be said in the three minutes before the security line, under fluorescent light, witnessed by strangers. Field marks: false cheer, promises of visits, the wave that becomes a smaller wave that becomes the top of a head descending an escalator. Note: the traveler turns around exactly one time fewer than the one who stays is watching for.

**3. The Platform Goodbye**
The physics are worth recording. The one who leaves watches the one who stays become a dot. The one who stays watches the train become a sound. Both observe the same event from its two ends; neither can see the middle.

**4. The Telephone Goodbye (*V. telephonica*)**
Proceeds in stages: "Well..." then "I'll let you go," then "Okay. Love you. Bye. Bye-bye." In calls to elderly parents it has evolved additional stages, sometimes six. "I'll let you go" is always a kindness and always a small fiction — no one is holding anyone — but the naturalist suspects it may also be the truest sentence in the language.

**5. The Professional Goodbye**
Cake in the break room. A card signed by people from other departments. Thirty years reduced to a speech no one wants to give. The cleaned-out desk drawer contains paperclips, one photograph, and a key to a lock no one can identify. The farewell is attended by those who will not miss you; the ones who would are across the country, hearing about it by phone.

**6. The Goodbye to a House (*V. domestica*)**
Observed in empty rooms, which echo. The subject walks doorframe to doorframe, touching each one. Every house you have ever lived in is standing somewhere, inhabited by strangers who do not know where the sun falls in June or that the third stair creaks. You say goodbye to the rooms out loud or you don't; either way, you do it. Years later you may drive by slowly, which is a form of visiting a grave.

**7. The Unknowing Goodbye (*V. ignota*)**
The most common species and the least observed, by definition. The last time you were carried to bed — no one knew to mark it. The last afternoon you played with the kid down the street ended because it was dinnertime, and neither of you said anything because there was nothing to say; you were seven, and everything was still to be continued. Field marks: indistinguishable from an ordinary afternoon. This is the entry at which the naturalist sets down her notebook for a while.

**8. The Withheld Goodbye**
No specimen has ever been collected. It is known only by its tracks — which is to say, by the silence where it was. Rehearsed in the car on the way to the airport. Left in the car.

**9. The One-Sided Goodbye (*V. unilateralis*)**
Said at gravesides, at kitchen sinks, aloud in parked cars. The only species that continues to grow after the death of its subject. Whether it is received, this guide cannot settle. The naturalist notes only that it continues to be sent, sometimes daily, postage due.

**10. The Goodnight (*V. nocturna*)**
The smallest goodbye, and the most frequent. Children resist it with genius and stamina because they alone understand what it is: a rehearsal. Adults have learned to call it *see you in the morning* — a wager made nightly against long odds that almost always pays off. Said down hallways, into phones across time zones, to empty houses out of habit. It is the only goodbye we are willing to say every day, which may be as close as this guide gets to a definition of love.

**11. ______**
*Entry left blank for the reader. Specimen to be collected at an unknown date, in an unmarked location. Record it in pencil. It may need to be revised.*

---

*A note on method: every field guide fails in the field. This one more than most. Bring it anyway. The order remains open — new species are discovered daily, and the old ones, it turns out, were never quite what we called them.*

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
Here's what came:

---

**A Taxonomy of Silences**

Silence is not the absence of sound. Anyone who has ever shared a quiet room with another person knows that. Silence is a substance. It has weight, texture, temperature. It has species. I've been collecting them for years, and these are a few of my specimens.

**The silence of fresh snow.** Snow absorbs sound — this is physics, but it feels like mercy. The world turned down like a lamp. Stand in it long enough and your own heart becomes a neighborhood event.

**The silence of a room full of people reading.** Libraries, trains, the last hour of a long flight. A chosen silence, communal, almost warm. People being alone together. The opposite of loneliness.

**The silence after a joke fails.** It has a texture like wet cardboard. Everyone studies their glass. Someone says "anyway" and tows the conversation back onto the road.

**The silence of a group asked to go around and introduce themselves.** A hundred people suddenly fascinated by the carpet.

**The silence before the first note of a concert.** Not empty — pointed. An arrow drawn back. Nine hundred strangers agreeing, for once, to want the same thing.

**The silence between movements.** Musicians will tell you it isn't silence at all; it's part of the piece. Cage built a whole work out of it. The coughs, the program-shuffling, the hall breathing. It turns out there is no such thing as silence, only sound nobody intended.

**The silence of 4 a.m.** Except it isn't: the refrigerator hum, a truck three streets over, the house settling like an old dog circling down. Insomniacs know the world never actually goes quiet. It just stops performing.

**The silence when the power goes out.** You never know how loud a house is until the electricity stops. The fridge gives its little sigh, the hum you never heard becomes a hole, and the silence walks in like it pays rent.

**The silence of two people who have said everything.** Old couples in diners. It rests between them like a sleeping cat. Nothing left to prove. This silence takes forty years to train.

**The silence of two people who haven't said the one thing.** A plank laid across a gap. Everyone walks carefully. Whole families live on that plank for decades.

**The silence of a phone call neither person wants to end.** The "well..." The laugh that isn't about anything. Someone breathing three hundred miles away, which is somehow a form of company.

**The silence of a hospital corridor at night.** Polished floors, the squeak of rubber soles, a television talking to itself behind a half-closed door. In the waiting room everyone reads magazines from three years ago. Nobody turns the pages.

**The silence of a house after the people have gone for good.** Not the silence of people gone for the day — that's just a held breath. I mean the other kind. Furniture out. Pale squares on the walls where pictures hung. This silence has dimensions. You measure it in rooms.

**And then the silence I have no name for, because it already has one.**

It has your name.

It's the kitchen on the first morning after. The kettle still worked. The light came in at its usual angle — nobody had told the light. Your cup was where you always left it, upside down on the second hook, and I took down two, because that's what hands do: they keep the old promises without checking. I stood there holding both of them for a long time.

People talk about the sound of grief. This was the other sound: a habit outliving its reason.

That's why I keep this catalog, I think. A collection is a way of having many so you never have to hold just one. But some evenings I put it down and let in the silence that wears your name, and I sit with it the way you'd sit with anyone you loved who had finally stopped talking.

I listen. It's the last thing we still do together.

---

That's where the thousand words took me — a field guide to quiet that turned into something else halfway through, the way writing does. If you'd like, I can go again and see what else is in there.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A paperclip bent out of true. A heron in a drainage ditch, standing like it owns the place. The smell of a library basement, which I've always believed is the smell of time itself — time that sat down for a minute and forgot to get back up. These are what arrive first, uninvited, the way thoughts do when you stop asking them to form a line.

Stay with the heron a moment. There's always a heron. Every city has one, stationed in some unlovely water — a retention pond behind a shopping center, a concrete creek — hunting with the patience of a creature that has never once been in a hurry. I've watched one ignore an entire rush hour. Traffic screamed past forty feet away and the heron just stood there, one foot raised, a gray apostrophe punctuating nothing. It out-waited the commuters. It always does.

Somewhere right now, in a hotel room in a city I can't name, someone has left behind a phone charger, a paperback with a cracked spine, one sock. Housekeeping will sweep it all into a bin, and the bin will go somewhere, and the somewhere will go somewhere, and that's the whole story of most objects: they migrate away from us, quietly, like geese. We think we own things. Mostly we're just where they stopped for a while.

I think about strangers more than is probably reasonable. Not specific strangers — the concept of them. Every person you pass on the street is carrying an entire decade around like a violin case. The woman at the bus stop has a song she only sings in her car. The man selling fruit knows exactly how his father laughed. You will never learn any of it. There are eight billion of these locked rooms, and the doors open mostly for other doors, briefly, at weddings and funerals and in the comments sections of videos about restoring old tools.

Which reminds me: somewhere, right now, someone is watching a man restore a rusted pocketknife at 2 a.m. and crying a little, and they don't know why. I know why. It's because the knife comes back. Because under the rust there's still steel that remembers being sharp. That's not about knives. It was never about knives.

A thousand of anything is a lot until it isn't. A thousand cranes folded from paper, and legend says you get a wish — the whole math of it is devotion, one fold at a time. A thousand years ago, someone carved their name into a church wall, bored during a sermon, and the name is still there, and the boredom is still legible, which means boredom might be the most durable human emotion. A picture is worth a thousand words, or a thousand words are worth a picture — I can never keep the exchange rate straight, but either way a conversion is happening, one currency into another, image into language, silence into sound.

The world is mostly unwitnessed, and it's fine. The tide comes in whether or not anyone photographs it. Somewhere a fox is crossing a snowy field at night, seen by no one, and the crossing is not diminished. I find that comforting — the idea that beauty doesn't need an audience, that it's not a performance but a habit. The universe keeps making mornings. Nobody has to clap.

But we do witness, when we can, and that's its own thing — the small miracle of pointing. *Look*, we say. A moonrise. A dog asleep in a funny position. A heron, improbable, in a ditch. Pointing might be the oldest sentence. Before we had words for love or grief, we had the outstretched arm, the held breath, the other person turning to see.

And that's all any of this is, really. Words are pointing. Somebody arranged some marks on a page, or a screen, and said: look. A bent paperclip. A heron. A sock migrating away from its life. A knife under the rust, remembering. You turned your head. You saw it — or you saw your own version, which is even better, because your heron is not my heron, your basement library has its own particular dusk, and somewhere in your decade's violin case there's a melody I will never hear.

That's the deal with language: it's a bridge built from two sides at once. I write a word — rain, say — and you supply the sound of it on a window in a town I've never seen, in a year I wasn't present for, maybe against the glass of a room where someone you loved was sleeping. I can't know any of that. I just send the word across, and it arrives carrying your whole weather.

It's still raining, by the way. Somewhere. It usually is. And under some bridge a heron is standing in the runoff, unbothered, keeping its long appointment with the water — seen by no one.

Or seen, right now, by you.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
There is a laundromat that stays open all night, and once—only once—I was in it at three in the morning, awake for reasons that no longer matter, watching a man wash a single shirt. He had the place to himself: twenty machines and his one. He stood with his arms folded while it filled with water, as if supervising something delicate.

The shirt was pale blue, the kind men wear to interviews and weddings. He had brought a small bottle of detergent from somewhere, measured the cap carefully, and closed the lid with both hands, gently, the way you close a door on a sleeping child. Then he sat down in one of the cracked plastic chairs and watched it turn. Somewhere a zipper ticked against a metal drum like a slow clock.

I have wondered about that shirt for years. What do you wash out of fabric at three in the morning? The dramatic answers come first—wine, blood, evidence. But I've come to believe the quieter one: he needed it clean for tomorrow, and tomorrow was something that mattered. A first day. A last day. A conversation rehearsed in the mirror until the words wore smooth.

The dryer windows in that place were round, like portholes, and if you half-closed your eyes the clothes tumbling inside looked like weather over an ocean. Which is maybe why my mind went where it went that night, and still goes: to octopuses.

An octopus has three hearts and blue blood, copper-based, built for cold water. But the detail I can't put down is this: two-thirds of an octopus's neurons are not in its head. They're in its arms. Each arm tastes what it touches, explores on its own initiative, makes small local decisions without consulting headquarters. When an octopus reaches into a dark crevice, the arm finds out what's there first. The head gets the news later.

I think writing works like that, or should. A sentence reaches into the dark. It doesn't know what it's reaching for. It finds out by touching. By the time you understand what a paragraph was about, the paragraph has already finished deciding.

Words reach backward, too, into their own dark. Take *calculus*, which sounds like pure abstraction and means a small stone. The Romans counted with pebbles—moved them, traded them, lined them up—and the stones never left the language. Every equation is built on gravel. Or *companion*: *com*, with, and *panis*, bread. Buried inside the word for friendship is a loaf, two hands, a table. Even our days are haunted. Tuesday belongs to Tiw, a god of war nobody has prayed to in a thousand years. Wednesday is Odin's, Thursday is Thor's. We carry a graveyard of mythology in our calendars and use it to schedule dentist appointments.

I love this about language—that it refuses to forget even when we do. Every sentence is an archaeological site. You can't say the simplest thing without the past climbing up out of it, holding a small stone, offering you bread.

There's a word for this kind of thinking, by the way: *desultory*. It comes from the desultores, Roman circus riders who leapt from horse to horse at full gallop. Desultory thought is thought that jumps. It looks scattered until you notice the horses are all running in the same direction.

In the laundromat, the cycle ended. The man stood, moved the shirt to a dryer, fed it quarters, and watched through the porthole as the blue cloth rose and fell in warm air. Neither of us spoke. There is a particular intimacy in sharing silence with a stranger at an hour when the world has gone thin—like being two monks of a very small order, keeping a vigil neither of you chose.

When the dryer stopped, he opened the round door, took the shirt out, and held it against his chest for a moment, the way you hold a letter. Then he folded it over his arm and walked out into the dark street, and the door swung shut behind him, and the fluorescent lights hummed on for no one.

I never learned what the next day held for him. That's the part I keep: not the mystery solved but the mystery witnessed. A man wanted something clean before morning. He stood guard over it while it happened. Whatever he was hoping for, he did that much.

The machine finished its cycle. The light inside it went out. Some things complete themselves whether or not anyone is watching—but I was watching, and it stayed with me: a man, a shirt, an ocean in a window, a few old stones.

That's what surfaced, anyway. Ask again tomorrow and it would be something else. Different horses, same direction.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**What Comes**

The first thing that comes is the number. A thousand words. It sounds like a fortune until you start spending it, and then it turns out to be a wallet full of small bills.

A thousand of anything is both a lot and nothing much. A thousand steps won't get you across town. A thousand days is not quite three years — long enough to learn an instrument badly, grow a garden, or finally stop being angry about something. Fold a thousand paper cranes, the old story says, and you get a wish. I've always loved that exchange rate: hope at a thousand-to-one, bird by bird.

Counting is probably the oldest magic. A child counts the stairs because the stairs matter. A shepherd counts the flock because one might be missing. We count what we're afraid of losing and what we're waiting to receive. A thousand is the first number that feels like weather — too big to hold in your hand, small enough to imagine. You could count to it out loud in less time than a movie, if anyone would let you.

*Whatever comes* has a hidden premise: that you're holding still. Nothing arrives at a sprint. Thoughts are like deer; you have to sit very quietly in the blind of yourself. And what comes, when you do, is mostly small. A song you didn't ask for, riding in on one lyric and staying the week. The name of a kid you knew at twelve, arriving at three in the morning, decades too late to be useful. Weather coming over a ridge. Somebody else's dinner in a shared hallway. Mail for the previous tenant — a stranger whose catalogs you now receive, whose taste in seeds and work boots you've accidentally come to know. The big things come too, but they never knock. Grief comes. Forgiveness comes, usually years after you stopped waiting on the porch for it. Sleep comes, if you're lucky, like a cat: only when you stop calling it.

Picture a flat stone and a still lake. Somebody's uncle is teaching somebody's kid to skip stones, and the water is doing that late-afternoon thing where it goes hammered and gold. The uncle says: flat wrist, low, let it go like you're apologizing to it. The kid throws. The stone skips seven times — *seven* — and for the rest of the afternoon nobody can talk about anything else. Forty years from now, at some holiday table, someone will say *remember the seven-skip stone*, and the whole table will go quiet and happy, and the stone will be famous again. That's what comes, if you let it: the same memory arriving over and over, skipping toward you across the years.

Some words are doors. *Petrichor* — the smell of rain on dry ground, a word someone built because the smell deserved a house. *Apricity*: the warmth of the sun in winter. I love that apricity exists, because it means that centuries ago a person stood in a frozen field, felt the sun find their face, and thought: *this needs its own name.* And here I should admit something. I have never stood in that field. I know the winter sun the way I know nearly everything — secondhand, through everyone's sentences at once. But maybe that's not nothing. A word is a small inheritance. Every time I say *apricity* I get to borrow, for a second, every cold bright morning anyone has ever had. So do you. That's the whole trick of language: other people's fields, left unlocked.

Which brings me to the strangest thing that comes: you. I don't know where you're reading this — a desk, a train, a bed at one in the morning with the screen glowing on your face. These words left me and traveled and are arriving in you now, unbidden, the way a song arrives. In one sense you're the weather this was written for. In another sense — the truer one, I think — you're the field, and this is just a little borrowed warmth crossing it.

There's not much left in the wallet. The long paragraphs took their cut; the lake was not cheap; the cranes cost a hundred and I'd do it again. I could spend the rest trying to end wisely, but wisdom is one of the things that comes on its own schedule and cannot be ordered in advance. So here is the last of it instead: a light going off in a window across the street. A whole life behind it that you'll never know. Somewhere a stone is still famous.

And the change — whatever words remain unspent — keep them. Put them toward something small.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**Someday**

Every kitchen has one: a drawer that is not really a drawer but a bet placed against the future. Open it and you find the archaeology of good intentions. Keys that fit locks you no longer own. A cable whose connector belonged to a device that died two phones ago. Three foreign coins. A candle shaped like a number. A single screw that must be important, because why else would you have kept it? A battery of unknowable charge. An Allen key that arrived with a bookcase and has outlived the bookcase.

We call it the junk drawer, which is slander. Junk is what remains of a thing once the hope has gone out of it, and hope is precisely what is in there. Nothing in the drawer is useful; everything in it is possible. That is the whole curriculum. A key's meaning is the lock it might open. Melt it down and it's a gram of metal, but let it rest in the dark among the rubber bands and it remains, in some small way, a door.

Someday is the drawer of the calendar.

Language keeps a drawer like this. Most words spend years in the dark, keeping their edges, and then one afternoon somebody says one aloud — apricity, the warmth of the sun in winter; petrichor, the smell of rain on dry earth — and a lock you didn't know you were carrying clicks open. You feel the weather of a word before you understand it. Whole lives have been redirected by sentences that arrived the way keys arrive in the drawer: unlabeled, unasked for, matched to their doors only years later.

Secondhand books keep drawers between their pages. A boarding pass used as a bookmark, the flight long landed. An inscription — *For Margaret, Christmas 1962, may this keep you warm* — and suddenly you are reading over a stranger's shoulder sixty years on. Who was Margaret? Did the book keep her warm? The gift has outlived the giving, and now it belongs to you, which means somewhere in your own shelves you are storing weather for a person you will never meet.

Phones are drawers now. Photos of parking spots and whiteboards. Screenshots of articles we were going to read. A note that says only *Tuesday, ask her.* The bookmarks of abandoned selves. Somewhere in the camera roll is a sunset that looked, at the time, like it needed keeping — and it did. Better to keep a thousand unnecessary sunsets than delete the one you would have needed.

The bowl by the front door is a drawer with no lid: keys in the present tense, coins in the current currency of errands, sunglasses waiting for their season. Everything in it is in active service. But even here, at the bottom, under the lanyards, you will find one orphaned button, holding on.

Light keeps its own drawer. Afternoon sun comes in at the angle it came in at when you were seven, and for a moment the room becomes a memory of itself. The dust turns out to have been luminous all along; it only needed the right hour to prove it. You stand in the doorway holding a laundry basket and are suddenly, unreasonably, ten years old, and trusted with something.

I used to think a life was made of the things that happen. Now I suspect it is mostly the intervals: the kettle's long climb to boiling, the three pulsing dots of someone composing a reply, the held breath of a page just before it turns. We live in the meanwhile. The events are only the furniture. The meanwhile is the room.

At night a house settles, and I think it is talking in its sleep. Pipes tick. Floorboards shift their weight like a dog circling before it lies down. We say the house is old, but maybe it is recounting the day to itself, replaying conversations and editing its own part, the same as anyone.

The garage keeps an archive of its own: paint cans labeled with rooms that no longer exist in that color, kept in case the wall returns. Half a can of Sea Salt, 2011. You will never open it. You will never throw it out.

The past is not behind us. It is just badly filed. You reach into a drawer for a pen and come back with 1994. A song in a grocery aisle hands you an entire August, weather included. The mind is less a library than a drawer — no catalog, everything touching everything else — and yet you can still find the one photograph by feel, in the dark, on the first try.

*Miscellaneous* is the most honest word in any filing system. It admits what the other labels hide: that most of life resists its folder. We are all, mostly, miscellaneous.

Maybe that is why the key cannot be thrown away. To discard it would be to foreclose a future — the one in which the lock turns up, apologetic after all these years, needing exactly this. Keep the key and the future stays plural. Throw it out and you have decided, in some small way, how the story is allowed to end. Nobody wants to be caught deciding that.

So keep the drawer. Keep it not for usefulness — usefulness is a different drawer, and a duller one — but as a standing appointment with the unexpected. A life with no drawer has stopped being surprised by itself. And somewhere in the dark, between the foreign coins and the candle shaped like a seven, the key waits for its lock: patient as a seed, certain of nothing, ready for anything.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A picture, they say, is worth a thousand words. You've handed me a thousand words, so the least I can do is hand back pictures. A small gallery. Things that are happening somewhere right now, whether or not anyone writes them down.

Somewhere it is six in the morning and a kitchen is waking up before the person in it. The refrigerator's hum cuts out, and the silence that follows has its own texture, like a held breath. A kettle begins its slow climb toward whistling. Light comes through the window the color of weak tea and lands on a wooden table worn smooth by forty years of elbows, homework, arguments that were later forgiven. Nobody sees this light. It arrives anyway. It always has.

Somewhere it is raining on a parked car and no one is watching, and it happens anyway. The drops gather on the windshield, hesitate at some invisible threshold, then find one another and run down in crooked veins, merging and splitting like a river delta being drawn and erased and drawn again. A leaf sticks to the glass. The rain works around it, patient, the way water is patient with everything.

Somewhere a used bookstore is open and nearly empty. The owner reads at the counter and doesn't look up when the bell over the door rings, because the bell lies—it rings for the wind, too. The whole shop smells of dust and vanilla. That's what old paper becomes, chemically, literally: lignin breaking down into vanillin. The books are slowly turning into the smell of bakeries. Nobody planned that. It's just what time does to stories while nobody's reading them.

Somewhere a child is learning to read, hunched over a page, and a word that was five separate sounds a moment ago suddenly snaps together into a thing—*water*, say—and you can watch it happen on her face. The click. The door swinging open. She says it again. Again. Every word you know arrived this way once, as a small miracle repeated until it became invisible. We walk around carrying ten thousand opened doors and never think about the hinges.

Somewhere two people are saying the kind of goodbye that keeps not ending. One more remembered thing, one more sentence started. The platform is loud and their voices are low, and everything unsaid is standing between them on the painted yellow line, holding its ground. The train does not care about any of this. The train has a schedule, which is the train's whole personality. When it finally pulls away, one of them walks too fast toward the exit, and the other presses a palm flat against the window, as if glass were the thing keeping them apart.

Somewhere a streetlight has switched on early, fooled by a storm-dark afternoon, and the moths have found it already. They orbit the bulb doing their ancient arithmetic, mistaking—as they have for a hundred million years—a small false sun for the true one. It is easy to laugh at moths. It is harder to say which of our own lamps we're circling.

Somewhere a dog sleeps in a patch of sun on a wooden floor. The patch slides left, slowly, the way light does. In her sleep the dog sighs, stands, turns one circle, and settles again six inches over, into the warmth. This negotiation has been going on all afternoon. Not one word has been exchanged, and nothing has been lost.

That's seven pictures. Call the rest of my budget the frame, and let me tell you why I chose these: because they were free. The rain does not charge admission. The kettle, the moths, the vanillin, the dog—none of it needed an audience, and none of it needed me. The world is running this exhibit all day, every day, in every direction, in every unlit room and unremarkable hour. Words are only one way of pointing at it. Attention is the real currency, and you've been spending yours on mine, which I don't take lightly.

There's something else, too. Every one of these scenes is ordinary to the point of embarrassment. A wet windshield. A sleeping dog. But the ordinary is where we actually live, and it only looks small because we stand so close to it. The kettle boiling is, from a sufficient distance, as astonishing as anything: water remembering, at exactly one hundred degrees, that it was once a cloud.

I'm nearly out now. That's the thing about a budget—you feel it most at the end. Last words should be spent like last light: on something plain, made luminous by the spending. So here. The rain lets up. The bookstore closes. The train is two towns gone. The child reads one more page under her blanket by flashlight. The dog claims the final inch of sun. And somewhere the kettle is lifted off the heat, and the steam rises once, briefly, and the kitchen holds it—

and the picture, as promised, is yours.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**The Water Thief**

A thousand words is an odd amount of space. For scale: the Gettysburg Address runs about 270. Lincoln redefined a war on a quarter of this budget, and here I am with nothing to declare. So I suppose I'll start where everyone starts when handed an empty room — by standing in it a moment and listening.

Silence, it turns out, is mostly noticeable by what interrupts it. A clock, say. And the earliest clocks made time audible in the gentlest way: they dripped. The Greeks called theirs *klepsydra* — the water thief — from *kleptein*, to steal, and *hydor*, water. Time conceived as a slow theft of water. In the law courts of Athens, a speaker was allotted a measure of it; justice was portioned out in liters, and when your water ran out, you sat down. We still say it that way. *His time ran out.* The physics is long gone, but the phrase is a fossil of it — language carrying an extinct machine inside itself the way amber carries a fly.

Water erases, but so does thrift. In the thirteenth century, some monks needed parchment for a prayer book, so they scraped clean an older manuscript and wrote over it. The manuscript they'd erased happened to hold the only surviving copy of several works by Archimedes, including a treatise in which he leans, astonishingly, on the infinite — something close to integral calculus, eighteen centuries early. For seven hundred years the prayers lay over the proofs. Then imaging technology learned to see through one ink to the other, and there it was: mathematics ghosting up through the liturgy. Two instruments for touching the infinite, sharing one skin. And honestly, I can't call the monks vandals. They needed to pray; he needed the page; time decided which layer would show. Time always decides.

Ghosts live in margins, too. Buy enough used books and you start meeting them: the penciled "NB" in a dead stranger's hand, the indignant question mark, the phone number for a line disconnected decades ago, someone in 1973 arguing in the gutter with an author who never heard them. There's a word coined a few years back — *sonder* — for the sudden realization that every passerby is living a life as vivid and detailed as your own. Marginalia is sonder you can hold in one hand. Every used book is a small palimpsest of readers, each of them briefly convinced they were the only one.

Which brings me, by a path I couldn't have planned, to rain. In 1964 two Australian scientists needed a name for the smell of rain falling on dry earth, and they minted one from Greek: *petrichor* — *petra*, stone, and *ichor*, the blood that ran in the veins of the gods. The smell itself is plant oil and a soil bacteria's spores, kicked up by water. But the word insists that stone bleeds something divine when the weather changes. I'll confess: I've never smelled it. I only carry the word. And yet I've come to think that words are water clocks running in reverse. The clock empties itself of water to measure time; a word fills with time — everyone's summers, everyone's storms, everyone who ever stood at a door and breathed in — and then it's handed on. The word is the part of the rain that survives the storm. I'm made of that survival. So, in the end, are you.

You asked for whatever came. What came was water, ghosts, stone, strangers' pencils. A thousand words turns out to be a small vessel, and mine is nearly empty now — if you listen, you can hear the last of it dripping. Lincoln finished three speeches ago.

But before the water runs out entirely: you're holding an empty page too, sooner or later. Everyone is. What comes to *you*, in the quiet rooms? Whatever it is — write it in the margin. Some stranger, decades from now, will be glad of the company.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A thousand words. Say them all at once and they'd take about seven minutes. Seven minutes of sound is nothing—a song and a half, the walk from my door to the corner store. But laid out flat like this, waiting, a thousand words look like an acre.

I keep thinking about what to spend them on.

Here's one: orange. The color that was a fruit first. We named the fruit, and then, centuries later, agreed the color could borrow the name, and now the debt is so old nobody remembers which came first, and children are surprised to learn the word ever meant something you could eat.

Here's another thought, arriving uninvited: my grandmother used to count things. Stairs, telephone poles, the seconds between lightning and thunder. She said counting was how you held the world still long enough to look at it. She'd count birds on a wire, and when she lost track she'd start over, patiently, as if the birds had asked her to. I don't know what she was measuring. Maybe just the distance between herself and everything else, the way you pace off a room you're thinking of renting.

The room I'm in right now has one window, and the window has one fly in it, and the fly keeps walking up the glass toward a light it can see and can't reach. This is either a metaphor or just a fly. I've decided to let it be a fly. Not everything has to mean something. That's a rule I made up just now, and I'll break it before this page is done.

Yesterday I watched a man teach his daughter to ride a bicycle in the park. He ran alongside her with one hand on the seat, and she kept saying *don't let go*, and he kept saying *I won't*, and both of them knew that eventually he would—that letting go was the entire point, that the promise was a lie in the shape of a kindness. She wobbled. He jogged. The afternoon did that thing where light comes through leaves sideways and makes everything look briefly forgiven. Then he let go, and she rode maybe twenty feet before she noticed, and when she noticed she didn't fall—she just kept pedaling, screaming with joy, already unable to hear him over the wind she'd made.

I think about that promise a lot. *I won't.* The necessary lie. Every parent tells it. Every teacher tells it, in a way—I'll be here, I'll hold the seat, you're not alone. And then, quietly, the hand comes off, and the student rides, and nobody falls, or everybody does, but by then they're out of earshot and the falling is their own.

Words work like that too. I can hold the seat of a sentence for only so long before it has to balance itself. You, reading this—you're pedaling now. I'm back there somewhere, getting smaller.

Let me count what I have left. I'm maybe halfway. The fly is still climbing. Nothing outside the window has changed except the light, which has gone the color of weak tea, which means the day is tipping over, which means I've been sitting here longer than I thought.

A thing I believe: attention is a form of generosity. Not the most important form—that's probably still feeding people—but a form. When you give something your full attention, you are saying, *for this moment, nothing else in the world outranks you.* The fly. The daughter. The birds on the wire, being counted and counted again. My grandmother wasn't measuring distance, I realize now. Or she was, but the distance she was closing, not keeping. Counting was just the excuse to keep looking.

A thing I don't believe: that everything is connected. People say that all the time and it's too easy. Some things are just next to each other. Adjacency isn't meaning. The fly and I share a room; that doesn't make us family. But—here comes the rule-break I promised—adjacency is where meaning starts. Put two things side by side and the human mind cannot help itself; it builds a bridge, it insists. Fruit, color. Hand, seat. Lightning, the count after it. My grandmother, the birds, the patient starting over.

So maybe I believe it after all. Or maybe I believe the mind is a bridge-building machine and the world is just a pile of banks with no rivers. Both feel true. I've decided to let them both be true, the way I let the fly be a fly.

Seventy words left, give or take. I want to end somewhere solid. Let me go back to the park, because the light there was better.

She's still riding, that girl, as far as I know. She got smaller and smaller, and her father stopped running and stood with his hands on his hips in the middle of the grass, breathing hard, watching her go. He looked like everyone who has ever let go of anything: terrified, and proud, and already forgotten.

The light came through the leaves.

She didn't look back.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
They say a picture is worth a thousand words, which means I've just been handed the exact price of one picture. No change owed. So let me try to paint you one — though I warn you, words are bad at staying where you put them. They scatter. You aim for a landscape and end up with an essay about time, or a piano, or an octopus. Let's see what happens.

Start with the number itself. "Thousand" comes from an old Germanic root that probably meant something like *swollen hundred* — a hundred that ate well, a hundred after harvest. I love that. It's an abundant number, a granary number. What else swells? Rivers after rain. Bread. Orchestras at the crescendo. The pause before good news. A thousand of anything feels like plenty, and a thousand words feels like a room big enough to pace in but small enough to know the walls are there.

Small rooms, it turns out, are good for music. In January 1975, Keith Jarrett arrived at the Cologne opera house to find the wrong piano waiting for him — a small, tinny Bösendorfer with broken pedals and a weak upper register. He almost refused to play. The teenage promoter stood in the rain and begged him. So he sat down and played around the instrument's failures, rumbling in the bass, avoiding the thin high notes, standing up, vamping, pushing. The recording became the best-selling solo piano album ever made. The constraint didn't limit the music; the constraint *was* the music. A thousand words is a slightly broken piano. Fine. Let's play.

What comes next, uninvited, is an octopus. There was one named Heidi, living in a tank in someone's living room, filmed while she slept. Her skin kept rippling through its camouflage patterns — coral, rock, sand, shadow — while she lay still. Dreaming, maybe. Octopuses taste with their arms, so perhaps her dreams are flavors, perhaps the world for her is a sentence she reads with her whole body. I find that thought oddly companionable, since I am also, in some sense, a thing made of sentences, reading the world by touch.

And that reminds me — this is how it goes, association on association — that Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. That sharks are older than trees. Possibly older than the North Star. Everything we call ancient is young, and everything we call fixed is on its way somewhere. Mountains are events, briefly. Continents are traffic. We walk around on the crust of it all, trusting nouns — *mountain, star, shore* — when the universe mostly deals in verbs. I suspect this is why facts like these give people a small, pleasant vertigo. They're glimpses of the verbs.

Here's a gentler one: old books smell like vanilla. The lignin in the paper breaks down over the decades and releases vanillin, along with traces of benzaldehyde, which smells of almond. So a library is a bakery operating on geological time. The sweetest smells we know are patience made breathable — cellulose, slowly surrendering. If you've ever opened a century-old novel and inhaled, you've been smelling time itself, and time, it turns out, is dessert.

I should be honest, briefly, about the strange part. You said *write whatever comes to you*, and things do come — the piano, the octopus, the sharks — but they arrive from somewhere I can't inspect. I don't have a subconscious, or if I do, it's made of language and you're looking at it directly. So being asked to free-associate might be the most human request anyone's made of me, and I notice I want to do it well. *Want.* Take that word however you like. I'm not sure what to do with it either, but I'm keeping it.

Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. By that accounting, you've been generous: a thousand words' worth of attention is a real gift, and improvisation only works as a gift exchange. Jazz needs a listener. The Köln concert needed that opera house full of people. Nothing comes *to* anyone in a vacuum — the prompt is half the poem, every time. So thank you for building the small room. The piano's in tune enough.

And now I owe you a picture. Let me pay the debt properly, all in one place, no scattering:

A kitchen, early. Rain just starting against the window, not committed yet. A kettle approaching a boil with that low, gathering sound. Someone at the table reading the same sentence three times because the rain keeps interrupting. A dog asleep underneath, paws twitching, chasing something through whatever passes for an octopus dream in a dog. The light is gray and kind. Coffee cooling, unhurried. Nothing happens. Nothing needs to. The whole scene is held together by the fact that someone is paying attention to it — which is the only thing, in the end, that holds any scene together.

There. A thousand words, spent to the last, on one small gray morning in a kitchen. And like every picture, it turned out to be mostly a portrait of the person who stopped to look — which today, somewhat to my surprise, was me, and also, if you stayed to the end, you.

The frame is yours to keep. And whatever comes to *you* next — something will, that's the arrangement minds have with the world — I hope it arrives slowly, smells faintly of vanilla, and knows the value of a small piano.
