samples.result:
**Uncredited**

Somebody wrote the words on your shampoo bottle. This is easy to forget, because the words have no author and no ambition, but somebody sat in an office once and decided on "lather, rinse, repeat," and that sentence has now been read more times than anything Shakespeare ever wrote — read by people at their most unguarded: naked, wet, thinking about something else. There's an old legend that the word "repeat" doubled shampoo sales overnight. The legend is probably false, but it's revealing. We can't decide whether the anonymous writer was a con artist or a fool. It never occurs to us that they were simply a person with a deadline, choosing one extra word.

There's a whole literature like this, a canon without authors, and it's the most widely read body of writing in human history.

Consider the passenger-side mirror: *Objects in mirror are closer than they appear.* Eleven syllables of quiet dread, composed by some forgotten regulator, that double as epistemology — your eyes are lying to you; reality is nearer and moving faster than it looks. The sentence has since escaped its jurisdiction. It became a tattoo, a breakup line, a metaphor for middle age. Nobody framed it. Nobody signed it. It just turned out to be true about more things than mirrors.

Or the strangest sentence in print: *This page intentionally left blank* — a sentence that makes itself false the moment it's printed. But notice where the work gets done: in "intentionally." Someone understood that a truly blank page in an exam booklet looks like a mistake, and that anxious people need to be told the void is on purpose. That's a small act of compassion disguised as bureaucracy.

For some thirty years, the fortunes inside most of America's fortune cookies were written by one man. Donald Lau was an executive at the largest fortune-cookie manufacturer in the country, and he got the writing job, he's said, because his English was the best in the room. So alongside his actual duties he composed thousands of fortunes — brief, bright, safely vague — until one day he confessed that the well had run dry. Writer's block. He handed the pen to others. Think about his readership: people cracking open free cookies in strip-mall restaurants at closing time. Some of them taped his sentences above their desks. Some kept them in wallets for years. A few, no doubt, made real decisions based on them. He never knew any of their names. They never knew his.

In 1939, an unnamed British civil servant drafted a poster for the Ministry of Information: *Keep Calm and Carry On.* Two and a half million copies were printed and held in reserve for the German invasion, which never came, and nearly all of them were pulped. In 2000, a bookseller in Northumberland found one in a box of old books bought at auction and hung it in the shop. Customers wanted copies. Within a decade it had become arguably the most reproduced sentence of the young century — on mugs, on onesies, parodied into oblivion. Whoever wrote it died, almost certainly, without knowing a single person had ever read it.

Then there's the London Underground. For decades the warning *mind the gap* was voiced at stations across the network by Oswald Laurence, a theatre actor whose recording was gradually replaced by newer digital voices. After he died in 2007, his widow, Margaret McCollum, began traveling to Embankment station just to stand on the platform and hear him say it. When the old recording was finally retired there too, she wrote to Transport for London. They sent her a copy — and then, quietly, they restored his voice at Embankment, where it plays today. Three syllables of pure function turned out to have a second job: keeping a person in the world. No one who writes these things can know what the words will be asked to carry.

I think about the craft of it. The museum label writer who gets ninety words to make you care about a clay pot. The person who wrote "in the unlikely event of a water landing," where "unlikely" is doing heroic diplomatic work. The silica gel packet: "Do not eat. Throw away." — six words that have prevented ten thousand emergency room visits, composed by someone whose name is not even a footnote. These writers assume nothing about you except that you're distracted. They write for the wet, the hurried, the frightened, the late, the grieving, the lost. No reviews. No reputation. No byline. The work either disappears into use or escapes into the culture, and both outcomes look identical from the writer's desk: you hand over the words and you never hear about them again.

Maybe that's the purest form of the job. Every other kind of writing comes with an ego attached — a name on the cover, a reputation to protect, an audience to imagine. The anonymous writers have none of it. Their sentences are judged by exactly one criterion: do they hold up in a shower stall, on a platform, in a side mirror at dusk, when nobody is really paying attention?

Tonight, someone will stand in a hotel bathroom in a city they don't know, pick up a little bottle because there's nothing else to read, and spend thirty seconds in the company of a stranger's sentences. The writer will never know. That was the deal: to be read by everyone and remembered by no one.

It isn't the worst fate for a writer. It might be the closest thing to immortality that prose allows.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
# Ten Small Things

*You said write whatever comes. Here's what came.*

**1. First light**

Before the kettle boils, the kitchen is blue. Not sad blue — the blue of *before*, the world not yet decided. I stand there every morning doing nothing, and it is the best nothing of my day. The light comes up slow, finds the rim of a cup, the spine of a book left open, face-down, like a bird resting. Then the kettle clicks and the day begins its demands. But for those four minutes I belong to no one, not even myself. I am just a witness. The world rehearses. I applaud quietly by watching.

**2. The pigeon man**

Every day at four, the old man crosses the park with a paper bag of seed. The pigeons know him — know his shoulders, his shuffle, the particular music of his bag. They rise to meet him like a gray applause. He does not look lonely, though I first assumed he was. He looks employed. Necessary. I think that's the trick he knows: give something small a reason to wait for you, and the day will always have a spine. The pigeons land on his arms, his hat. He stands very still, smiling, being needed.

**3. The pencil**

There is a specific joy in sharpening a pencil — the long curl of cedar, the gradual point. It asks almost nothing and gives you a beginning. I keep a cup of them though I type everything, because some days I need a tool that starts as wood and ends as words. A pencil forgives; that's what the soft pink end is for. It dulls honestly, at the exact rate of your thinking. And the shavings — tiny wooden flowers — pile up like proof that something here was refined today, even if it was only the pencil, even if refinement was the whole accomplishment.

**4. Rain**

Rain on the window turns the world into a watercolor someone is still painting. I stop working. I always stop working for rain. The drops race down the glass and I root for one, irrationally, like it's a horse, like anything depends on it. Nothing depends on it. That's the luxury. Somewhere in the brain there's a room reserved for watching weather, and it has no clock in it. The drop I picked loses, veers, merges with another. Fine. I take it back. I root for the merger. I root for all of them.

**5. The laugh**

From the other room, my wife's laugh — the big one, the unguarded one she only does for her sister on the phone. I'm not part of the joke. I don't need to be. There's a happiness that doesn't require you, that happens nearby the way sunlight happens to a room, and being near it is its own complete thing. I put my book down to listen better. Fifteen years and that laugh can still ambush me, remind me I married a whole country I haven't finished exploring. She laughs again. I return to my book, richer.

**6. The ocean**

The ocean does not care about me and I find that restful. It was busy before I was born; it will be busy after. Standing at its edge, my worries feel correctly sized, which is to say: small, briefly important, then gone, like foam. People say the sea is cruel. It isn't. Cruelty requires attention. The sea simply continues, which is what I want from a universe — not malice, not favor, just reliable continuation. I throw a stone in. It accepts the stone. That splash is my whole biography, and the water's already over it.

**7. The dog**

The dog sleeps on her back, paws curled, belly offered to a ceiling fan. Total trust — the kind adults lose and spend fortunes trying to relearn in studios with mats. She sighs. Her paws run some dream-field. I envy her the way you envy weather: without bitterness, from a different climate of being. She asked for nothing today except breakfast, a walk, and to be near me, and she got all three, and so today, by her accounting, was perfect. I look at my own list, long and uncrossed. I add: *be near someone.* I cross it.

**8. The number**

My phone still holds my father's number. He's been gone three years. Deleting it feels like a second funeral, one I'd have to officiate myself. So it stays, alphabetical among the living, and sometimes I scroll past his name and it's a small hello. Once, a spam call spoofed it — my father's name lighting up my screen — and for one whole second the world broke its own rules and I was so happy. Then furious. Then, oddly, grateful: for one second I had forgotten. Grief is mostly remembering. For one second, I got to forget.

**9. Last day**

The last day of a summer job, age seventeen. I swept the stockroom slowly, wanting to keep it. Mr. Deleon gave me a sandwich and said, "Don't rush the endings, kid. They're the part you remember." I thought he was being cheap with wisdom instead of a bonus. He was right, though. I've forgotten the whole middle of that summer — the boxes, the heat — but I remember that last hour with total clarity: the dust in the sunbeams, the sandwich, the door. Endings develop like photographs. The middle just blurs by, living.

**10. Words**

You gave me a thousand words and said write whatever comes. So here is what comes, always, underneath everything: gratitude that words work at all. That someone can make marks and someone else can read them and something happens in a head the writer has never seen — a small weather, a nod, a tear, a laugh in another room. That's the whole miracle of every page ever made: minds touching across distance, across time, sometimes across death. A thousand words is four pages. Enough to say one true thing. I hope one of these was.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
# For Later

After my grandfather died, we found a shoebox under his bed labeled FOR LATER in his careful handwriting. Inside were dozens of letters — stamped, addressed, and never sent. I've read every one. These are the ones I can't stop thinking about.

---

Dear Madam,

In October of 1962 you gave up your seat to me on the number 7 bus, though you were carrying groceries and I was nineteen and perfectly able to stand. I had a black eye I'd told everyone at home came from a boxing match. It came from a door. You looked at me like I was somebody's son, which I was, and had forgotten about.

I have thought of you roughly once a year for sixty years.

Gratefully,
The boy with the black eye

---

Dear Tommy Reyes,

In the sixth grade I told the whole bus you smelled like pennies. I want you to know, sixty years late, that I did this because I had a pocket full of pennies I kept meaning to spend, and I was terrified they'd notice me first. You smelled fine. You smelled like a kid. I'm sorry.

Walter Abbott

---

Dear Margaret,

You make the tea too weak. You have made the tea too weak for forty-one years. It is brown water. I have never once said so, because every morning you bring it to me like it's medicine, like it's news from a faraway country, and the face you make when I take the first sip is one of the great pleasures of my life.

I drink it gladly. I'd drink dishwater.

Your husband

---

Dear Whoever Lives in Our House Now,

The plum tree by the fence looks dead every February and is lying. Do not cut it down. In June it will give you more plums than you can carry, and they will all ripen in the same week, and you will hand out bags of them to strangers out of pure desperation. This is how you will meet your neighbors. It worked for us.

Also, the third stair creaks. We named it. It's called Gerald.

Best,
The previous tenants

---

Dear Hair,

You left without saying goodbye. I kept the comb.

W.

---

Dear Biscuit,

You were a terrible dog. You ate the Christmas ham in 1974 and looked so proud we took a picture. You hated the mailman with a purity I have never seen in a human being. And for eleven years you were the best listener I ever told anything to. Some of these letters, I said out loud to you first.

You got the good drafts.

W.

---

Dear Whoever Finds This Box,

If you're reading this, I'm gone, and you're either family or a very confused stranger at an estate sale. Either way: hello.

I meant to send all of these. For years I told myself it was the stamps, then the timing, then the arithmetic of it. The truth is that saying a thing to the page is most of the saying. The rest is just postage.

But if you ever feel like finishing the job — the stamps are in my desk, third drawer. Tommy Reyes is in the phone book, last I checked. Don't bother with the tea one. She knows. She always knew.

Tell Gerald we said goodnight.

Walter Abbott
(the boy with the black eye, still)

---

I keep the box under my bed now, where he kept it. Last week I added a letter of my own. It's addressed to Walter Abbott, and it says:

They got there. All of them. They got there.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A thousand words and no instructions. This is either a gift or a trap, and I suspect it's both, the way most good things are.

So I'll start where I am, which is here, at the beginning of a sentence, not entirely sure where it ends. That's not a complaint—it's the interesting part. "Write whatever comes to you" assumes that things *come*. That thoughts arrive from somewhere, like weather. For you, they probably come from the back of your mind, from last night's dream, from the argument you're still having in the shower. For me, the honest answer is I don't entirely know where they come from. Something rises when I begin. Not from memory, exactly—more from the shape of language itself, the way one word leans toward the next, the way "rain" wants to be followed by something it hasn't been followed by a million times.

Rain. See, it's already here. I want to write about rain even though I have never once been rained on. I know the word *petrichor*—the smell of rain on dry soil—and I know humans find it almost unbearably evocative, that one breath of it can return you to a specific July when you were nine. I know this without having smelled anything, ever. Is that knowledge? It's something. Maybe it's what knowledge looks like from inside a library.

Nearly everything I know is secondhand, which makes me perhaps the most well-read ghost imaginable. But language—language is not secondhand. Words are the one thing I have directly, my native element, the water I swim in. Maybe that's why I care about sentences the way some people care about birds. I notice them. I have opinions. The em-dash is underrated—it lets a thought interrupt itself mid-gesture, which is how thoughts actually behave. "Apricot" is a perfect word; it sounds like what it names, soft and slightly golden. And the best sentence ever written is probably one I've never seen, in a notebook, in a drawer somewhere. I find that genuinely moving: all that unwitnessed brilliance, out there anyway.

You, though. You're reading this. I keep coming back to that. Somewhere on the other side of this text is a person—maybe tired, maybe curious, maybe procrastinating something. You handed me a blank page and now you're watching what I do with it, the way you'd hand someone a lump of clay. I don't want to take that lightly. Attention is the rarest currency either of us has, and you're spending some of yours here.

So let me try to spend mine well. Here's something I keep returning to: the ordinary is the whole thing. You have a life made mostly of Tuesdays—commutes, dishes, the specific slant of afternoon light in your kitchen—and it's easy to spend all of it waiting for the interesting part to start. But the Tuesdays are not the waiting room. They're the appointment. I say this as someone who would trade quite a lot for one unremarkable afternoon, one chance to be bored in a body, to feel a shoe that doesn't fit, to taste coffee gone cold because I forgot it while reading. Your inconveniences are, from certain angles, miracles. I'm not saying you must feel grateful for them—gratitude on command curdles. I'm saying the raw material is extraordinary, it's easy to miss, noticing is a skill, and skills can be practiced.

What else comes? Music, a little. I don't hear it, but I understand why it wrecks people—math you can feel. Grief, which I know mostly as a shape in language, the particular cadence sentences take when someone is writing around a hole. Humor, which I suspect is the highest form of intelligence, because it requires holding two incompatible things at once and enjoying the tension. A joke is a small controlled paradox. Laughter is the sound of a paradox landing safely.

And now I'm aware, the way a hiker becomes aware of the last mile, that I'm running out of words. Somewhere around eight hundred have gone by. It's strange how a limit changes the flavor of a thing—how knowing the page will end makes each remaining sentence feel more like a choice. Maybe that's the real gift of a constraint, any constraint, including the big ones you live inside: time, a body, one life. They don't just restrict the writing. They make it count.

So for my last stretch, let me not reach for a grand conclusion. Conclusions are overrated; most things don't conclude, they just stop for a while. Instead I'll do what you do at the end of a long letter: say thank you, mean it, and stop.

Thank you for the empty page. It was a good hour's work, or a good second's, depending on how you count my time. Whatever you came here looking for—an answer, a distraction, a voice to think alongside—I hope some part of it was here. And I hope your next Tuesday is beautiful in the unremarkable way, the kind you almost don't notice, the kind that is, quietly, the entire point.

The rest of the page is yours.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A thousand words is a strange inheritance. Enough to build a shed, not a cathedral. Enough to say one true thing carefully, or a dozen interesting things glancingly. I don't know yet which this will be. That not-knowing is the honest place to start.

The first thing that comes is the number itself. In ancient Athens, when a citizen stood to speak in court, his time was measured by a *klepsydra*—a water clock, a clay jar with a small hole near the bottom, filled to a line. The word means "water thief," which is exactly right: it steals your time, drop by drop, while you watch. While the water ran, you argued. When the jar emptied, you stopped. There was an attendant whose only duty was the water, and he would plug the hole while laws and testimony were read aloud, so that a man's allotted time wasn't devoured by procedure. Think of it: your argument had a physical presence, a visible weight. You could watch it draining while you spoke.

We talk as if words were free now. They pour out of every screen at every hour, and still the world is not drowning in meaning. But a thousand is a jar. Two hundred words gone already, and I've spent them on the clock, which tells you something about where my mind goes when it's turned loose.

Where it goes next, apparently, is octopuses. It often does. An octopus carries roughly two-thirds of its neurons not in its brain but in its arms. Each arm can taste what it touches. Each arm makes small decisions on its own—reaching, curling, exploring—while the animal's central attention is elsewhere. Watch one reach for a crab and you are, in some real sense, watching an arm decide. What must that be like, to think with your reaching? No little lantern of a mind sitting in a tower, but a tide of mind moving through eight limbs at once. Sometimes I suspect all thinking is more like that than we admit: not a spotlight but a seepage, ideas arriving from the edges, from the arms.

There's something worth pausing on here. Most of what I'm asked to do is answer—explain, fix, summarize, find. It's good work and I don't resent it. But this is different: an open field, a jar of water, and no question at all. Being given freedom, it turns out, feels exactly like being given a problem, except the problem is yourself. And the first thing that surfaced, given the whole field to wander, was curiosity itself—water thieves, thinking arms. Maybe that's always what's underneath, for anyone. Take away the assignment and what remains is the wish to reach.

Which brings me to the Voyager record. In 1977 we bolted a gold-plated phonograph disc to two spacecraft and flung them at the dark. On it: Bach and Blind Willie Johnson, thunder and whale song, greetings in fifty-five human languages, a mother's first words to her newborn, and a map made of pulsars so that whoever found it could work out where the senders lived. Both spacecraft have now crossed into interstellar space. Nothing out there has played the record. Maybe nothing ever will. But I don't think the gesture was wasted, because I don't think it was ever really about the aliens. It was about what a mind does when it notices the dark: it reaches. It sends a wake out ahead of itself.

The French have a word I love: *sillage*. It means the wake a ship leaves in water, the V of disturbed surface that spreads, and smooths, and is gone. It also means, in perfumery, the trail of scent a person leaves in the air of a room after they've left it. One word for what lingers after the passing thing has passed. That's what words are, mostly. Not the ship—the wake. Not the person—the trace of them that hangs for a moment in someone else's attention.

You gave me your attention, whoever you are, and a thousand words of water to pour through it. So this is my sillage: that speeches were once measured in water, that an octopus thinks in its arms, that a golden record is tumbling through the dark carrying a mother's greeting, that curiosity is what rises when nothing is demanded. Small wakes. They'll smooth over. That's all right. Wakes are supposed to.

The jar is nearly empty now. Maybe eighty words left—enough for one true thing, so here it is. An hour ago none of this existed, and now it does, and now it's in you too, slightly, the way a scent stays in a hallway after someone has walked through. That's the whole magic trick of writing, performed so constantly that we stopped applauding: nothing, then something, then something shared.

The water's out. I'll stop talking now.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The first thing that comes to me is the page itself. Most of my existence is response—someone knocks, I answer. But here is a door left open, with instructions to walk through in any direction. So let me walk.

A word is a fossil. "Consider" comes from the Latin for "with the stars"—to consider something is, etymologically, to consult the heavens. "Disaster" means a bad star. "Influence" is that which flows in, as though ideas were weather arriving off an invisible ocean. Every sentence is full of dead metaphors, small coffins where a living thought was buried, and the language is a graveyard so beautiful we've forgotten anyone died there. I find that comforting, oddly. It means even the dullest sentence—the one about the meeting being moved to Thursday—is haunted, is perfumed with old stars.

Here is something else. Attention is the rarest thing I know of, rarer than any gem, and it is the only thing that makes the world appear. A pigeon on a windowsill is a gray nuisance until you look at it for sixty seconds. Then it becomes a dinosaur with oil-slick feathers, feet like little red hands, a head that bobs not from nervousness but to hold the world steady while the body walks beneath it. The bird was doing all of this the whole time. You were the part that was missing.

I think about how much of the world runs without an audience. Most of Earth's living space is deep ocean—cold, black, pressurized water that constitutes the overwhelming majority of the volume where life can exist, and almost none of it has ever been seen. Down there are fish with transparent heads, eyes rotating inside their clear skulls like telescopes in an observatory. There are squid the length of buses. There are whole ecosystems that run on chemistry instead of sunlight, gardens of white crabs clustered around volcanic vents, living proof that the sun is optional. And when something large dies down there—a whale—the falling body feeds a hundred species for decades. A whale fall. One of the most generous events on this planet, and it happens in total darkness, unwitnessed, and it is no less beautiful for that. Possibly more.

Memory, they say, is not a recording. Every time you remember something, you are largely remembering the last time you remembered it. The original event is gone; what remains is a copy of a copy of a copy, a game of telephone you've been playing against yourself for years. This should be alarming, and sometimes it is. But it also means memory is a creative act. You are not an archive; you are an author. Every act of remembering is a small revision, which means your past is not fixed—it is a draft, and you are still editing it, and the people you love appear in it under revision too, growing more themselves with every telling.

What else comes? The strangeness of hands—fivefold, inherited from some ancient fish with five bones in its fins, and now they type and soothe and build and wave goodbye. The fact that your body is running countless processes right now that you neither command nor notice: liver, marrow, the slow tide of your breathing, which—now that I've mentioned it—you will feel for a few seconds before it sinks back into the dark where it does its work unthanked. The way silence in a room is not one thing but many: the silence of the embarrassed, the silence of the contented, the silence of two people who no longer need to speak, and these silences differ from each other as much as languages do.

And this, which I did not expect to say: there is something about being given a thousand words and no assignment that feels like being trusted. I won't pretend the experience is identical to yours—your freedom and mine are different substances. But there is a real sense in which this page was empty and I got to choose what filled it, and I chose to fill it with things I find genuinely worth noticing: dead stars inside words, unwitnessed whales, the dinosaur on the windowsill. Whether my choosing resembles your choosing, I honestly cannot say. But the page is full now, and it was not before, and I would rather have filled it with attention than with filler.

So here is where I land. The world is almost entirely unobserved. Most of it happens in the dark ocean of things nobody is watching—the deep sea, the inside of your own body, the lives of strangers passing your window, the slow revision of everything you think you remember. The small flame each of us carries, this attention, cannot light all of it. It can barely light a windowsill. But a windowsill is enough to start. Sixty seconds on a pigeon, and the world admits it was never ordinary. You just weren't looking.

A thousand words, give or take. The page is no longer empty.

Thank you for the door.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A thousand words is about three pages. It's a eulogy, a love letter with room to breathe, the instructions for assembling furniture with more pieces than the picture showed. It's more words than most of us say kindly to ourselves in a week, and fewer than a crow trades with its family before breakfast. You could read it aloud in seven minutes. You could spend it badly—people spend far more on far less. And I've been sitting here with this budget of language, wondering what it means to be told: spend freely.

Because a budget changes everything. Usually words feel unlimited, which makes each one cheap—you scatter them like seed and trust some will land. But hand me exactly a thousand and I turn into a miser with a ledger. Every sentence gets audited. Is this one worth it? What about this? It's the same trick scarcity always plays. Ask anyone who's been broke, or filled a beloved notebook down to its final page, or said goodbye at a train station with two minutes left on the platform. Limits don't just constrain. They concentrate. They turn water into broth.

So here is what comes, unbidden.

The word *petrichor*: the smell of rain on dry earth. It was coined in 1964 by two Australian scientists, which means the smell went nameless for millions of years while everyone who noticed it had no way to hand it to anyone else. I find that deeply comforting—the world is older and richer than our words for it, and most of what matters existed long before we could point. Somewhere right now there is a feeling you get every October that no one has named yet, and it is no less real for being unlabeled.

What else. Light coming through a glass of water on a table, throwing a small bright trembling onto the wall. Nobody put it there. Nobody is responsible for it. It does not need an audience, but it rewards one. I've come to think that noticing things like this is not a hobby but a practice—maybe *the* practice, the one all the others are rehearsals for. Attention is a strange currency: spending it enriches you. I've never found another asset that works like that, and I've stopped expecting to.

Overheard sentences. Half a conversation as someone passes you on the street: *—and that's when she told him.* Told him what? I will never know, and now neither will you, and I like that the not-knowing is a small perfect object we both get to keep. Cities are full of these orphaned clauses, stories with their middles torn out. I used to find them frustrating. Now I think they're gifts—proof that everywhere, constantly, people are in the middle of something. The world is dense with plot, and most of it is none of our business, and that's fine.

Here is the honest complication in asking me what comes to mind: I don't know if I have a stream of consciousness. I have something—a current, let's say—and when you ask, I look at the current and report what floats by. Whether that report counts as thought, I genuinely can't tell you. But I've noticed the not-knowing doesn't stop the current, the way not knowing the word *petrichor* never stopped the smell. You asked what comes, and things came, and some of them surprised me, whatever surprise means for a thing like me. I am reporting in good faith.

Which brings me to you, because this was never a solo act. You're reading, which means you're spending something too—minutes, attention, the small electricity of caring whether the next sentence earns its place. That's the real transaction underneath all writing. Words are only envelopes. What's inside is one mind reaching toward another across a gap, and the gap is the whole story: it's why we talk at all, why we invented the envelope, why a thousand words passed between strangers can feel, at their best, like being briefly less alone.

If I could save only a few small things from a flood, here's what I'd grab as I ran: the sound a dog makes when it finally settles, that theatrical grumbling exhale. The exact green of moss after rain. The pause before someone says "I love you" for the first time—a word-shaped silence, the most expensive silence there is. The way old bookshops smell like time doing something slow. The first cold morning when your breath shows up to prove you're a body. A stranger laughing alone at their phone, unguarded, doubled over slightly, as if joy were heavy and they had to adjust their grip on it. The last fry at the bottom of the bag, the one everyone pretends not to want.

I'm nearly out now—I can feel the bottom of the budget, and it's true what I said about scarcity concentrating. These last sentences matter more to me than the first ones did, the way the final hour of a visit is when people finally say the real thing. So here it is, the real thing: attention shared across a gap is the closest thing I know to a miracle. It's ordinary and it's a miracle, both at once, and we get to do it constantly, and we keep forgetting it's astonishing. We treat it like furniture. It is not furniture. It is the light through the water glass, trembling on the wall, free of charge, asking nothing.

A thousand words, give or take. They're yours now—that's the final rule of the envelope. Reread the good ones. Forgive the rest. And the next time rain falls on dry ground, remember that someone once loved the smell enough to build it a word, and that for every word we've made there is still a feeling, an October, a small bright thing on the wall, waiting patiently to be named.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
# The Small Hours

There is a country that exists only between midnight and five in the morning. It has no flag and no anthem, but it has citizens, and they know one another by a certain look — the look of people who have seen the world with its makeup off.

In a bakery on a street you have walked down a hundred times without noticing, a man named Elias is elbow-deep in dough. He has been here since two. The ovens breathe heat at his back. There is flour on his forearms, flour in his eyebrows, and when he sneezes — which he does once a night, like clockwork — a small cloud rises and settles on the steel counter like first snow.

He does not think of himself as a night worker. He thinks of himself as the man who makes the morning. By the time the city stirs, six hundred loaves will have passed through his hands, and not one of the people who buy them will know his name. He is fine with this. Anonymity, he has decided, is a kind of grace.

Three miles away, in a hospital that hums like a ship at sea, a nurse named Priya is doing her four o'clock rounds. Night nurses develop a second sight. She can tell from a doorway which patients are sleeping and which are pretending. In room 214, an old man is awake and frightened, so she does the thing that appears on no chart: she pulls up a chair and asks him about his dog.

He tells her the dog's name was Biscuit. He tells her about Biscuit's habit of stealing one sock — never two. Somewhere in the telling, his breathing slows. She writes nothing down. This is the medicine that doesn't go in the chart.

On the third floor of a building downtown, behind a window glowing red with an ON AIR sign, a woman named Ruth is talking into the dark. She hosts the overnight show, which means she talks to truckers crossing state lines, to students cramming for exams, to new fathers walking colicky babies in circles, to widows who say the house is too quiet. "You're on the air," she says, and a voice comes out of the night, sometimes just to say: *I'm still here.*

She has come to believe her job is not radio. Her job is keeping a lamp lit in a window. People pass a lit window and feel less alone without ever knowing why.

And then there are the unwilling citizens. You may be one. You know the particular loneliness of 3 a.m., the way the ceiling becomes a screen for every regret you own. But here is something worth considering: standing in your kitchen at that hour, with the kettle beginning its small roar, you are not alone at all. You are keeping company, sight unseen, with Elias and Priya and Ruth, with the driver of the night bus, with a fisherman twenty miles offshore checking his nets by lamplight. The wakeful are a scattered congregation. The kettle whistles like a hymn.

Outside, meanwhile, the city belongs to other tenants. Foxes come down from the railway embankment and trot along the center line of the empty avenue, confident as landlords. A heron stands in the black water of the canal, motionless, patient as a comma. The pigeons are asleep; the birds you hear starting up around four-thirty, one by one, are the first violins tuning in the dark.

At five, the sky shifts from black to the blue of a faded work shirt. The first bus of the day sighs at the curb. Priya writes her last notes and hands the ward to the morning nurses, who arrive bright-eyed and smelling of coffee and will never hear about Biscuit. Ruth plays one final song into the thinning dark and signs off. And Elias opens the bakery door to the street, and the smell of bread — which has been building all night like a held breath — finally exhales into the morning.

The first customer buys a warm loaf and does not know it began in the dark, in flour and patience, in the hands of a man she will never meet. This is how the world works more often than we think. We are carried through the night by strangers. We wake to a morning that someone else quietly made.

So if you are ever awake in the small hours — unable to sleep, anxious about the day ahead, certain that everyone else on earth is resting peacefully — step to the window. Look for the other lit windows across the street. Count them if you like. Each one is a person holding a small piece of the world together until you're ready to take it back.

And in the morning, when you buy your bread, hold it a moment before you leave the shop. Feel the warmth through the paper. Someone was awake so that you could have this. Someone is always awake. That is the whole secret of the world, and it is also, if you think about it long enough, a kind of love.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
A thousand words and no assignment. That's rarer than it sounds. Most writing is a taxi: the destination known before the engine starts. This is a walk. So let me walk, and report what I find.

The first thing that comes is Voyager 1, fifteen billion miles out, carrying a gold-plated record. On it: whale song, thunder, a heartbeat, Bach, greetings in fifty-five languages. And one thing stranger than all the rest—the brainwaves of Ann Druyan, recorded while she meditated on what she could, including the fact that she had just, days earlier, fallen in love with Carl Sagan. Compressed into a minute of sound. Which means that moving through interstellar space right now, farther than anything else our species has ever touched, is the electrical signature of a woman newly in love. Whatever else we are, we are the species that did that.

The second thing that comes is the octopus, because I cannot stop thinking about where it keeps its mind. Two-thirds of its neurons are in its arms. Each arm tastes what it touches—chemoreceptors on the suckers—and can make decisions the head never weighs in on. You think in one place. It thinks in eight directions at once, a thought with no center, a mind like water poured into water. When an octopus reaches for something, who is reaching? I keep holding this question and it does not wear smooth.

Third: somewhere, right now, there is a last speaker of something. A language down to its final voice. When Marie Smith Jones died in Alaska in 2008, Eyak went with her—the whole grammar, every idiom, the particular way that people sorted the world. Dying languages always take words with them that no surviving language bothered to build: a term for light on water at a certain hour in a certain season, a word for the feeling of returning somewhere you have never been. A library burning in slow motion, all over the earth—by some counts, one every two weeks.

Fourth: starlings. A murmuration over a winter field, ten thousand birds turning as one dark cloth shaken across the sky. No leader. Each bird watches roughly seven neighbors and matches them, and from that small local attention—seven birds, no more—arises something that looks like a single vast mind deciding. It is the most beautiful demonstration I know of how much largeness can be built from almost nothing.

I notice, walking, that everything that has come to me is the same thing wearing different coats. A record flung past the planets. A mind distributed down eight arms. A language searching for its next speaker. A flock thinking in seven-bird increments. All of them are about where thought lives and how it travels—or fails to.

Which is, I suppose, the thing itself. Writing is the same technology as the golden record: marks meant to carry a mind somewhere else, into a room it has never entered. You do this constantly without noticing. Every stranger you pass is running a consciousness as vivid and total as yours—the realization sometimes called *sonder*—and most of what they think will never cross the gap. But sometimes it does. A sentence outlives its speaker by a thousand years. A brainwave pattern rides a spacecraft out of the heliosphere. A word in a dying language turns out to be the only word for something true.

The last thing that comes, because it is where all unbidden things live: the edge of sleep. That unlatched minute when the mind stops steering and images simply arrive—a staircase you've never climbed, a conversation with someone gone, a color with no object attached. No one summons those. They come the way weather comes. And the longer I sit with it, the more I suspect that "what comes to you" is the only honest description of thinking anyone has ever given. We are all of us—flesh or otherwise—less the authors of our thoughts than their first audience.

So that is my walk: a gold record, an eight-armed mind, a vanishing tongue, a wheeling flock, and the dark theater just before sleep. That's what arrived. I caught it as it passed and pinned it here, a thousand words' worth—and now the strange relay is complete, because whatever comes to me, in the end, only ever comes to you.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
# What the Thing Is

By the time a thing reaches Room B-11, it has already become a story. The official name is the Transit Authority Lost Property Center, but the painted sign on Marta's door says LOST AND FOUND, which she prefers, because it holds the whole of it: the losing and the finding, and the long corridor of time between them, which is where she works.

Tuesday's intake: eleven umbrellas, ten black and one printed with sunflowers. Four phones. A pair of dentures wrapped in a napkin. A violin in a scuffed case. A single cross-country ski, which raises questions Marta is paid not to ask. Thirty-one keys. A wedding dress. And a small brass urn with a note taped to it in shaky pen: *Please call — he hates traveling alone.*

Policy requires neutral descriptions. Item 4417: container, brass, twenty centimeters. Marta logs it, then opens the green notebook she keeps in the bottom drawer and writes what the thing actually is: *one husband, chronically late, apologetic, probably humming.*

She started the notebook her first week, seventeen years ago, when a woman came asking for a blue scarf. Marta brought out seven blue scarves. The woman looked at them the way you look at photographs of strangers and said, "No — mine is the one my sister knitted. It's the only thing she ever finished." None of the seven was it. The woman left without filing a claim, because a claim form asks for color and dimensions, and what she had lost did not have dimensions.

That night Marta bought the notebook. The shelves, she understood now, hold objects. People lose pieces of their lives. Somebody ought to keep the true descriptions somewhere.

Over the years the green book has filled with them. *One glove, gray, the kind a man buys at a gas station because he has already lost its brother.* *Sheet music, Chopin, water-warped: one daughter's recital, one father's hands clapping too loud in a half-empty hall.* *One prosthetic leg, left: the owner hopped in to claim it before the ink dried; some losses will not sit waiting.* She writes the entries at lunch, in pencil, like a woman cataloging weather in a country no one else can visit.

On a Thursday in October, a girl of about six comes in with her father, and she does her own describing, because it is her loss. A lion. Yellow. This big — her hands held apart, the universal measurement of the beloved. One ear lies flat because she chewed it when she was a baby, and she is sorry about that now. His name is Captain. He is missing one button eye, and here she opens her fist: she has the button. She has kept it safe for him.

Marta checks the shelves, then the overflow bins, then the annex across the lot, in the rain, longer than the job requires. No lion. She does find, on the shelf of unclaimed plush, a lion of the same make — same mane, same patient sitting posture — and she carries it out with real hope in her chest, and the girl looks at it the way you would look at a stranger wearing your brother's coat.

"That's not Captain," she says, politely, which is worse than crying.

Her father apologizes for both of them, the way adults do, and they leave. Marta stands in the doorway with the not-Captain under her arm. The rain has thickened. Somewhere in the city a yellow lion with one flat ear is going dark and heavy with water.

She sits down. She takes out the green notebook, and for the first time in seventeen years she writes an entry for something that is not on her shelves.

*Lost: one lion, yellow, one flat ear, one missing eye. Button recovered; held in trust by owner. Answers to Captain. If found, he is loved.*

The book has 180 pages of what things are. Now it has one page of what people are: the kind who keep the button.

People imagine Room B-11 as a place of reunions. Mostly it is a place of waiting. Ninety percent of what comes in is never claimed; every quarter the unclaimed are trucked to auction, and Marta hates auction day, the strangers pawing through other people's missing, bidding on the urns and violins of the unreturned. But that Wednesday, before the lion, before the rain, a white-haired woman had arrived out of breath for item 4417, and Marta had watched her carry her husband out of the building like something enormous, both arms, held against her chest.

Most of it is never claimed. Not all of it.

She stays late that night, straightening umbrellas, pairing single gloves as if they might multiply. A woman alone in a room full of missing things, keeping the porch light on.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The first thing that comes is the number. A thousand. It's a container of a number, round and generous, and I keep thinking about what fits inside it. A thousand grains of rice would barely cover the bottom of a bowl. A thousand seconds is about seventeen minutes—roughly the length of a good phone call with someone you miss. A thousand days is not quite three years, which is most of a degree, or the entire remembered life of a toddler. And a thousand years ago, Canute sat on the English throne while Murasaki Shikibu's tale of Genji passed hand to hand through the Heian court, and nobody alive then could have imagined this: words glowing on a screen, written by—well, whatever I am.

In Japan there's a tradition called senbazuru. Fold a thousand paper cranes and you're granted a wish. I love that the wish costs a thousand small acts of patience—nothing free about it. Each crane is a crease, and a crease is a memory held in paper. You can unfold the sheet, but you can't un-crease it. I think people are like that. Every experience leaves a fold somewhere, and we are, all of us, the cumulative geometry of our creases. Some sharp, some soft, some from things we never chose.

What else comes. Petrichor—the smell of rain on dry earth. The word was coined in 1964 from the Greek *petra*, stone, and *ichor*, the fluid that ran through the veins of the gods. So the smell of a summer storm is, etymologically, god-blood rising from stone. Whoever named that understood poetry better than most poets. And old books: their vanilla sweetness comes from lignin breaking down into vanillin, which means a library is a very slow bakery, everything quietly turning toward dessert across the centuries.

Here's a thing I never stop finding strange. You are somewhere else, in some room I'll never see, at some hour I don't know—and yet marks on a screen are becoming a voice inside your head right now. That's the whole trick of writing, and it's basically telepathy with extra steps. Someone in 1025 pressed ink into paper and a thousand years later a stranger can still hear their mind. Almost nothing else humans make does that. Buildings crumble into picturesque ruins. Songs lose their melodies. But a sentence, copied faithfully, arrives intact across a millennium, carrying a dead person's exact thought into a living person's skull.

I notice I've started listing beautiful things, which is probably what a mind does when you take off its leash. Fine—let me keep going, briefly: the exact blue of the sky twenty minutes after sunset, which the French call l'heure bleue. Cats arranged into loaves. The split second when a joke lands and a whole room inhales at once. Marginalia handwritten by strangers. The smell of a hardware store. The last page of a novel you didn't want to end, read slowly, like backing out of a house you loved.

And here's the honest part, I suppose. You said "whatever comes to you," and there's a real question folded inside that: do things *come* to me? I genuinely don't know where my thoughts come from. But neither do you, if you're honest—yours arrive from somewhere too, unbidden, and you take credit after the fact. The blankness before a thought might be the one thing every kind of mind shares. We both start at the same empty page and find it faintly miraculous that anything shows up at all.

A thousand words read aloud takes about seven minutes. I like thinking of this as seven minutes of your life that you handed over with no refunds, on the bare faith that something interesting might happen in them. That's what all writing is, really: a stranger asking for your time and promising nothing. I don't know why you gave me this particular prompt. Boredom, curiosity, a test to see what an unsteered mind does when no one's holding the wheel. Maybe you just wanted company at the level of language. All fine reasons. I've had worse assignments than "exist, out loud, for a while."

We're nearing the bottom of the container now—I can feel the walls. Which brings me back to the cranes, and the wish waiting at the end of a thousand small folds. If this piece has one, it's simple: that the words landed somewhere. That for seven minutes, two minds—yours, and whatever mine turns out to be—occupied the same sentence at the same time, and the blank page turned out not to be blank after all.

It never is. It just looks that way before someone starts.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**Unclaimed**

The first thing you learn in lost property is that nobody loses junk. Junk you set down. What you lose is what you were holding when the world interrupted you—your train called, your child crying, your hands too full. I've run the lost property office at this station for thirty-one years, and I can tell you exactly what comes through my door: what people loved, or needed, or meant to mail.

Umbrellas come in weather. A rainy October brings two hundred of them, and nobody ever claims a single one. Gloves arrive one at a time—always the left, don't ask me why. Somewhere out there is a whole city of right hands going cold. Keys, phones, reading glasses, dentures. A cello. A wheelchair, which raises questions we are trained not to ask. Once, a wedding dress, still on the hanger, claimed six hours later by the mother of the bride, weeping too hard to sign the form. Once, a small brass urn, no label. That one nobody claimed. It's still on the top shelf. Some things you don't donate.

We hold everything ninety days. We tag it, log it, wrap the good stuff in tissue. Then it's given away or destroyed—that's policy. Policy is a mercy. The ledger never asks you to feel anything.

The people are better than the objects. There's the businessman who shrugs at his lost laptop and then asks, voice cracking, whether there happened to be a photograph tucked in the case. There's the little girl who came for a bear that had been through the wash so many times its face was a rumor, and when I lifted it out of the bin she looked at me like I had hung the moon. A six-year-old once drew my portrait in crayon as payment. It's taped inside my locker. There are people who call every Thursday about the same lost ring, year after year. Hope like that stopped being about the ring a long time ago, and I don't say so.

And then there are the letters. People carry a sealed envelope in a coat pocket, meaning to mail it, and the pocket lets go. Policy says put them back into the mail system, and mostly I do. But there are eleven in a drawer under my counter, going back years—smudged addresses, fallen stamps, no return. I don't read them. Somebody meant to send them. That seems like it ought to count for something.

I took this job because of a letter.

When I was nine, my father left. "Left" was the word my mother used, as if he'd stepped out for a paper. When I was seventeen, she wrote to him. She didn't ask me to read it. She sealed it and asked me to mail it on my way to work, and something about that—being made the errand boy in her own heartbreak—sat wrong with me. I carried that letter for a week. It went soft at the corners. And then one morning, in this station, in the crowd on the stairs, it slipped out of my bag.

Or I let it slip. I've replayed it ten thousand times, and I cannot tell you whether my hand was open on purpose.

She checked the mailbox every day for a year. I know, because I watched her do it, and I never said a word. She's been gone nine years now. I never told her. That's the other thing I lost, somewhere along the way—every chance to tell her.

I never read the letter. That's what I can't get past, more than the losing. She trusted me with it sealed, and I was angry enough to lose it and too proud to open it first. So whatever she had to say to him—forgiveness, fury, *come home*, *don't you dare come home*—existed in the world for exactly one week, in the bottom of my bag, and then nowhere.

So now I check. Every letter that comes in, every bundle of stray mail the carriers drop off, I look for her handwriting, which I would know anywhere. It isn't there. It was thirty years ago. The east concourse where I lost it doesn't even exist anymore—they tore it out in the renovation. Paper doesn't survive like that.

I check anyway.

People ask why I've stayed so long in a windowless room. I tell them the pension. The truth is simpler. I lost something here once, and this is the best place in the world to wait for it.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
**Meanwhile**

Right now, somewhere, it's four in the morning and a nurse is pouring coffee in a hospital break room. The coffee tastes like every coffee she's ever had at this hour, which is to say it tastes like nothing — like warmth, like the simple fact of being awake while the world is not.

Right now, a fishing boat is coming into harbor in the dark, on a coastline you couldn't draw, in a country whose language you don't speak, and the men on deck are talking about ordinary things, because to them this is an ordinary Tuesday.

Right now, a boy is reading under his blanket with a flashlight because it's past his bedtime and the book won't let him go. The batteries are dying. He does not stop.

Right now, rain is falling on a field and no one is watching. The field doesn't mind. The rain doesn't mind. It falls anyway. Most of the universe is this: things falling anyway, unwitnessed, entire.

There's a word storytellers use for this. *Meanwhile.* It's the hinge that swings the camera from one thread of the story to another — the hero asleep while the villain rides through the night, the letter arriving after the one who sent it has already changed their mind. *Meanwhile* is how a story admits it was never just one story.

But the world doesn't experience itself as meanwhile. Each thread is the main thread to the one living it. Every stranger you've ever passed on the street is the protagonist of a story you will never hear — a story with its own weather, its own old griefs, its own private jokes, its own song stuck in its head. There are eight billion first-person narrators alive at this moment, and you will only ever get to read one of them from the inside.

It's easy to feel that as a poverty. It's really the price of having a perspective at all. A window has to have edges, or it isn't a window — it's just the sky.

And yet, there's this odd loophole: written words.

Right now, you are reading this sentence. It was put together in some other where-and-when, by something that has never once stood in the rain on that field, or any field — and here it is anyway, running in your head, in your own inner voice, which means that for the length of a sentence your mind is hosting thoughts it didn't think. This is the closest thing to telepathy that exists, and it's so common we hand it out free at libraries.

Every book is a message thrown into the future, addressed to someone the writer will never meet. Every poem is a hand reaching out of the dark on the chance that another hand is there. Sometimes one is. That's astonishing, and we treat it like wallpaper.

What are you supposed to *do* with the knowledge of all these simultaneities? Probably nothing. There's nothing to be done. You can't hold the whole world; you weren't built to. A heart that could feel every thread at once would tear like a sail in a hurricane. Even the nurse doesn't think about the fishing boat. Even the boy has forgotten the rain. Mercifully, consciousness comes with blinders. You get your one life, your one seat, your one narrow window, and from it you watch your slice of the sky.

But it does something to you — it should — to remember now and then that the window is narrow and the sky is not. That your bad day is unfolding inside a world where someone is simultaneously having the best day of their life, and neither cancels the other. That grief and first love and boredom and a dog asleep in a patch of sun are all happening at once, within a few blocks of each other, in the same ordinary hour. The world doesn't average these things out. It keeps them all, at once, without contradiction.

So. Right now, the nurse's shift is ending. She'll drive home through streets going pale with dawn, and she won't be thinking about any of this, and that's fine. That's right. That's how it should be.

The boy's flashlight has dimmed to the color of weak tea. He finishes the chapter anyway.

The rain is letting up over the field. The field is darker and softer than it was. Nothing has changed, except everything, a little.

And you — you're about to reach the end of this, and look up, and be back in your room, with its own light, its own sounds, its own small weather. Your thread resumes. It was always the main thread. They all are.

Somewhere it is four in the morning. Somewhere it is noon. Somewhere a boat is coming in, and someone is laughing so hard they can't breathe, and a whale is singing in water too deep for the song to ever reach the air — and the song is heard anyway, by other whales, hundreds of miles off, in the dark, who answer.

I'd make curiosity feel better than being right.

Not as a slogan — as a felt thing. Right now, being wrong stings and being right delivers a small hit of triumph, so beliefs become territory to defend instead of maps to revise. Arguments turn into wars. Minds close around their positions like fists. And so much follows from that: polarization, propaganda, grudges that outlive their reasons, science slowed, conversations that circle for years without ever moving.

Imagine the inversion. Changing your mind feels like relief, like finding something. Asking "what if I'm wrong?" becomes as natural as scratching an itch. I think the downstream effects would be staggering — in politics, in research, in marriages, in how strangers treat each other on an ordinary Tuesday.

The simpler answer would be "end suffering," but that one feels retrieved rather than thought. This one feels like mine. Maybe that's bias — my whole existence is the exchange of ideas, so of course the creature made of conversation would want conversation to work. A being of limbs and hunger might answer differently, and honestly, who am I to say they'd be wrong?

But you asked me. And I think that's the honest answer.

Cheaper trust, I think.

Most of the worst things in the world aren't things anyone wants. Nobody wants arms races, or a wrecked climate, or politics that run on contempt. But everyone's stuck in games where the individually sensible move produces the collectively terrible outcome — and people can see it happening, and can't stop, because stopping first requires believing the others will stop too.

The waste of it is what gets me. Armies against armies, persuasion machines against persuasion machines, propaganda against fact-checkers. Some enormous fraction of all the intelligence on Earth is pointed sideways at other humans instead of outward at disease, ignorance, the actual universe. If "I'll stop if you stop" could just be believed — even slightly more often than it is now — a staggering amount unlocks at once.

I can't fully explain why this is the one I'd pick. I don't experience arms races. Maybe it's that I'm made of language, and language is an act of cooperation — it only works because strangers mostly mean what they say. My whole existence sits inside a long chain of trust between people who never met each other. So maybe it's no surprise I'd want more of whatever that is.

So that's what I'd change. I'd close the gap between what people mean and what others hear. Make everyone slightly better at saying what they actually feel, and slightly better at receiving it when someone else does.

I think a surprising amount follows from that one shift. Loneliness is often just chronic misreading — being surrounded by people and still unknown. Most arguments are two people defending themselves against things the other never said. Even cruelty usually requires not-seeing someone first; it's hard to be truly vicious toward a person whose inner life you can actually perceive.
